+// DERPMap describes the set of DERP packet relay servers that are available.
+type DERPMap struct {
+	// Regions is the set of geographic regions running DERP node(s).
+	//
+	// It's keyed by the DERPRegion.RegionID.
+	//
+	// The numbers are not necessarily contiguous.
+	Regions map[int]*DERPRegion
+}
+
+// DERPRegion is a geographic region running DERP relay node(s).
+//
+// Client nodes discover which region they're closest to, advertise
+// that "home" DERP region (previously called "home node", when there
+// was only 1 node per region) and maintain a persistent connection
+// that region as long as it's the closest. Client nodes will further
+// connect to other regions as necessary to communicate with peers
+// advertising other regions as their homes.
+type DERPRegion struct {
+	// RegionID is a unique integer for a geographic region.
+	//
+	// It corresponds to the legacy derpN.tailscale.com hostnames
+	// used by older clients. (Older clients will continue to resolve
+	// derpN.tailscale.com when contacting peers, rather than use
+	// the server-provided DERPMap)
+	//
+	// RegionIDs must be non-zero, positive, and guaranteed to fit
+	// in a JavaScript number.
+	RegionID int
+
+	// RegionCode is a short name for the region. It's usually a popular
+	// city or airport code in the region: "nyc", "sf", "sin",
+	// "fra", etc.
+	RegionCode string
+
+	// Nodes are the DERP nodes running in this region, in
+	// priority order for the current client. Client TLS
+	// connections should ideally only go to the first entry
+	// (falling back to the second if necessary). STUN packets
+	// should go to the first 1 or 2.
+	//
+	// If nodes within a region route packets amongst themselves,
+	// but not to other regions. That said, each user/domain
+	// should get a the same preferred node order, so if all nodes
+	// for a user/network pick the first one (as they should, when
+	// things are healthy), the inter-cluster routing is minimal
+	// to zero.
+	Nodes []*DERPNode
+}
+
+// DERPNode describes a DERP packet relay node running within a DERPRegion.
+type DERPNode struct {
+	// Name is a unique node name (across all regions).
+	// It is not a host name.
+	// It's typically of the form "1b", "2a", "3b", etc. (region
+	// ID + suffix within that region)
+	Name string
+
+	// RegionID is the RegionID of the DERPRegion that this node
+	// is running in.
+	RegionID int
+
+	// HostName is the DERP node's hostname.
+	//
+	// It is required but need not be unique; multiple nodes may
+	// have the same HostName but vary in configuration otherwise.
+	HostName string
+
+	// CertName optionally specifies the expected TLS cert common
+	// name. If empty, HostName is used. If CertName is non-empty,
+	// HostName is only used for the TCP dial (if IPv4/IPv6 are
+	// not present) + TLS ClientHello.
+	CertName string `json:",omitempty"`
+
+	// CertFingerprint, if non-empty, specifies the expected
+	// lowercase hex of the SHA-256 of the TLS server's offered
+	// certificate. If empty, the system default RootCAs are used.
+	CertFingerprint []string `json:",omitempty"`
+
+	// IPv4 optionally forces an IPv4 address to use, instead of using DNS.
+	// If empty, A record(s) from DNS lookups of HostName are used.
+	IPv4 string `json:",omitempty"`
+
+	// IPv6 optionally forces an IPv6 address to use, instead of using DNS.
+	// If empty, AAAA record(s) from DNS lookups of HostName are used.
+	IPv6 string `json:",omitempty"`
+}

response.body:
Code's fine, but I'm not a huge fan of negative flag names (including `--no-snat`). It inevitably results in double negatives, especially when defaults change over time.

@danderson, what do you think of `--snat=false` and making `--snat=true` the default?

My take is that I really like `--no-<flag>` as shorthand for turning stuff off, whereas `--flag=false` is fairly terrible.

I'm okay with that being an argument for using a different/better flag and CLI library, however, I don't particularly care how I get to specify `--no-<flag>`, as long as I do :). If you prefer the other form, I'm fine flipping it and waiting until I replace the libraries to get my `--no-` back.

Note: I'm not at all sure that toggling the DERP option works on Windows. I
don't think anyone ever tested it properly. Nowadays it would be more
helpful to have a --no-udp option instead.

In options.py, the standard is to write the docs with --no-style if the
default is on, and --style if the default is off. It would then produce a
dict with the negative removed (eg. there was an opt.style, and if the
usage message suggested --no-style, then opt.style defaulted to true
instead of false, thus avoiding double negatives in the code itself). I
like that generally but it doesn't work very well for us, where we're also
trying to persist things and the default value for every unspecified flag
should be false. (To add extra pain, I also screwed that up as ipn.Prefs
expanded, so the default value of some of the fields is *not* false.)

Anyway, --no-flag style is fine with me, but I prefer that the opposite
--flag style be silently available so that people can override settings by
adding things to the end of the command line. Dunno if the current
framework supports that.

ᐧ

+// fakeOS implements netfilterRunner and commandRunner, but captures
+// changes without touching the OS.
+type fakeOS struct {
+	t         *testing.T
+	up        bool
+	ips       []string
+	routes    []string
+	rules     []string
+	netfilter map[string][]string
+}
+
+func NewFakeOS(t *testing.T) *fakeOS {
+	return &fakeOS{
+		t: t,
+		netfilter: map[string][]string{
+			"filter/INPUT":    nil,
+			"filter/OUTPUT":   nil,
+			"filter/FORWARD":  nil,
+			"nat/PREROUTING":  nil,
+			"nat/OUTPUT":      nil,
+			"nat/POSTROUTING": nil,
+		},
+	}
+}
+
+var errExec = errors.New("execution failed")
+
+func (o *fakeOS) String() string {
+	var b strings.Builder
+	if o.up {
+		b.WriteString("up\n")
+	} else {
+		b.WriteString("down\n")
+	}
+
+	for _, ip := range o.ips {
+		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "ip addr add %s\n", ip)
+	}
+
+	for _, route := range o.routes {
+		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "ip route add %s\n", route)
+	}
+
+	for _, rule := range o.rules {
+		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "ip rule add %s\n", rule)
+	}
+
+	var chains []string
+	for chain := range o.netfilter {
+		chains = append(chains, chain)
+	}
+	sort.Strings(chains)
+	for _, chain := range chains {
+		for _, rule := range o.netfilter[chain] {
+			fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%s %s\n", chain, rule)
+		}
+	}
+	return b.String()[:len(b.String())-1]
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) Insert(table, chain string, pos int, args ...string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if rules, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		if pos > len(rules)+1 {
+			o.t.Errorf("bad position %d in %s", pos, k)
+			return errExec
+		}
+		rules = append(rules, "")
+		copy(rules[pos:], rules[pos-1:])
+		rules[pos-1] = strings.Join(args, " ")
+		o.netfilter[k] = rules
+	} else {
+		o.t.Errorf("unknown table/chain %s", k)
+		return errExec
+	}
+	return nil
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) Append(table, chain string, args ...string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	return o.Insert(table, chain, len(o.netfilter[k])+1, args...)
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) Exists(table, chain string, args ...string) (bool, error) {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if rules, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		for _, rule := range rules {
+			if rule == strings.Join(args, " ") {
+				return true, nil
+			}
+		}
+		return false, nil
+	} else {
+		o.t.Errorf("unknown table/chain %s", k)
+		return false, errExec
+	}
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) Delete(table, chain string, args ...string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if rules, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		for i, rule := range rules {
+			if rule == strings.Join(args, " ") {
+				rules = append(rules[:i], rules[i+1:]...)
+				o.netfilter[k] = rules
+				return nil
+			}
+		}
+		o.t.Errorf("delete of unknown rule %q from %s", strings.Join(args, " "), k)
+		return errExec
+	} else {
+		o.t.Errorf("unknown table/chain %s", k)
+		return errExec
+	}
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) ListChains(table string) (ret []string, err error) {
+	for chain := range o.netfilter {
+		pfx := table + "/"
+		if strings.HasPrefix(chain, pfx) {
+			ret = append(ret, chain[len(pfx):])
+		}
+	}
+	return ret, nil
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) ClearChain(table, chain string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if _, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		o.netfilter[k] = nil
+		return nil
+	} else {
+		o.t.Errorf("unknown table/chain %s", k)
+		return errExec
+	}
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) NewChain(table, chain string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if _, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		o.t.Errorf("table/chain %s already exists", k)
+		return errExec
+	}
+	o.netfilter[k] = nil
+	return nil
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) DeleteChain(table, chain string) error {
+	k := table + "/" + chain
+	if rules, ok := o.netfilter[k]; ok {
+		if len(rules) != 0 {
+			o.t.Errorf("%s is not empty", k)
+			return errExec
+		}
+		delete(o.netfilter, k)
+		return nil
+	} else {
+		o.t.Errorf("%s does not exist", k)
+		return errExec
+	}
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) run(args ...string) error {
+	unexpected := func() error {
+		o.t.Errorf("unexpected invocation %q", strings.Join(args, " "))
+		return errors.New("unrecognized invocation")
+	}
+	if args[0] != "ip" {
+		return unexpected()
+	}
+
+	rest := strings.Join(args[3:], " ")
+
+	var l *[]string
+	switch args[1] {
+	case "link":
+		got := strings.Join(args[2:], " ")
+		switch got {
+		case "set dev tailscale0 group 10000 up":
+			o.up = true
+		case "set dev tailscale0 group 0 down":
+			o.up = false
+		default:
+			return unexpected()
+		}
+		return nil
+	case "addr":
+		l = &o.ips
+	case "route":
+		l = &o.routes
+	case "rule":
+		l = &o.rules
+	default:
+		return unexpected()
+	}
+
+	switch args[2] {
+	case "add":
+		for _, el := range *l {
+			if el == rest {
+				o.t.Errorf("can't add %q, already present", rest)
+				return errors.New("already exists")
+			}
+		}
+		*l = append(*l, rest)
+		sort.Strings(*l)
+	case "del":
+		found := false
+		for i, el := range *l {
+			if el == rest {
+				found = true
+				*l = append((*l)[:i], (*l)[i+1:]...)
+				break
+			}
+		}
+		if !found {
+			o.t.Errorf("can't delete %q, not present", rest)
+			return errors.New("not present")
+		}
+	default:
+		return unexpected()
+	}
+
+	return nil
+}
+
+func (o *fakeOS) output(args ...string) ([]byte, error) {
+	want := "ip rule list priority 10000"
+	got := strings.Join(args, " ")
+	if got != want {
+		o.t.Errorf("unexpected command that wants output: %v", got)
+		return nil, errExec
+	}
+
+	var ret []string
+	for _, rule := range o.rules {
+		if strings.Contains(rule, "10000") {
+			ret = append(ret, rule)
+		}
+	}
+	return []byte(strings.Join(ret, "\n")), nil
+}

response.title: Opt-in default route to non-tailscale wireguard nodes: send all Internet traffic
response.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

There are a number of times where it is helpful to be able to route all traffic or some traffic via a normal wireguard node that is external to tailscale. A few examples would be if you use a VPN provider ( AzireVpn or TorGuard ) that use unmodified wireguard or if you have a router at a location that had wireguard built in but not tailscale. My use case is to use TorGuard or AzireVpn and say all traffic on this node that does not meet a rule should be routed out to TorGuard or AzireVpn. Ideally it would be great to be able to ticka  box to apply to multi nodes but i suspect i will need a different config or something per concurrent node connecting or something

**Describe the solution you'd like**

In tailscale UI i would be able to configure one or more external normal wire-guard nodes and the routes they handle or process. Then in the UI i could either specify the node they apply to if it can only be applied to a single node or maybe an ACL if it could be applied to multiple nodes. I suspect that would be controlled by the restrictions of wire-guard itself.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Having a single node centrally configured with the external vpn/wireguard node and routing all traffic there but this is not ideal for home use as i would either need a cloud server with a lot of bandwidth that everything routes though or manually try to configure each node where tailscale is installed.

**Additional context**

This would be especially useful for docker networks where you would like the networks to be able to talk to each other over wireguard but for it to route anything else out over a VPN provider. The other use case would be mobile devices that want to access say a home network but route anything else over a VPN provider instead of over an insecure network.

@@ -381,6 +383,7 @@ func (e *userspaceEngine) Reconfig(cfg *wgcfg.Config, routerCfg *router.Config)
 	}
 
 	e.logf("wgengine: Reconfig done")
+	e.logf("wgengine: new peer list: %s", strings.Join(peerKeys, " "))
response.body:
Usually this is the right thing to do, but in the case of this particular log message, because of how we want to use it, I think we want to do something slightly different. As written, this message will print out only when wireguard is reconfigured, so:
1. This might be too rare, if the network reconfigures. Processing eg. 1 hour or 1 day of logs is not guaranteed to include the peer list.
2. This might be too frequent. We'll reprint the peer list every time wgengine reconfigures, even if it hasn't changed.

What we want instead is:
1. It must print every time the peer list changes, right away, before any more Peers: lines get printed.
2. It must print at least every n seconds, so that we only have to analyze a relatively short chunk of logs and we'll be guaranteed that the message has printed at least once.

Thus, I'd suggest printing out the peer list right before the existing Peers: line. You'd want something like "if (not_printed_in_last_5_minutes) or (new_peer_list != old_peer_list) then (print new_peer_list)".

I'd rather not include extra words in a line that prints so frequently. I think it's fine to leave this prefix unmodified.

The new-style peers line will only print peers we're connected to, and which line up with the "peer list" array rather than the network map array. However, an analytics script can tell the difference between the two: if there are any "peer list" lines, then it's new-style, otherwise it's old-style. So you don't need to mark anything in this line.

+	var peerKeys []string
 	e.mu.Lock()

response.body:
From now on, we only want to print nodes we *are* connected to in the peers: log line, not every peer in the network map. That list will change more frequently than Reconfig() (which gets a list of all nodes in the network map, whether or not we've tried to connect to them yet).

The best place to generate (and print) the peerKeys list will be at exactly the same time as you print the peers: line. As a result, you probably want to remove this entire loop from this section, and manage the peerSequence separately at the point when peers: is printed.

commit.message:
wgengine: generate and plumb router.Settings in from ipn.

This saves a layer of translation, and saves us having to
pass in extra bits and pieces of the netmap and prefs to
wgengine. Now it gets one Wireguard config, and one OS
network stack config.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

wgengine/router: rename config.Settings to config.Config, make pointer.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

response.body:
I added a constructor to make this all nicer:

https://github.com/inetaf/netaddr/pull/35

little weird to see `Reconfig` five times on this line (`Reconfig`, `cfg`, `wgcfg`, `Config`, `routerCfg`), and then--surprise!- `Settings`. Especially since the variable of type `Settings` is called `routerCfg`.

Maybe it wants to be `router.Config` to match `wgcfg.Config`?

(random place to comment, but...)

router.Settings is pretty large and pointer-heavy to be a value type. (https://github.com/golang/go/wiki/CodeReviewComments#receiver-type)

Any objections against changing to passing it around by pointer everywhere instead? Then this could just be nil.)
Will update once merged in netaddr.
Sure, seems like a harmless rename. Added a followup commit that does this.

No objection. Started out smaller and I embiggened it while splicing it out from wgcfg.Config. Adjusted to a pointer type, with nil handled gracefully within router to mean "a config that removes most tailscale customization from the network stack".
I'd just drop the parameter names now (cfg and routerCfg). Also, the docs mention "The provided DNS domains" which is no longer applicable.

response.title: Support relaying a default route through Tailscale
response.body:
We support subnet routes. However, default routes fall prey to #144, so we can't relay all of a node's traffic through another node.

This is an obviously desirable feature, and we need to make it work. Filing this so we can track it in our user pain tracker, even though we can't fix it until #144 is done (which itself is blocked on #320 currently).

response.title: Changing hostname aliases crashes and reboots MacOS
response.body:
**Describe the bug**
Changing the hostname aliases the ACL section of the admin screen makes MacOS crash and reboot the machine.

**To Reproduce**
1. Tailscale client for MacOS is configured and up and running
2. On the ACL page in the admin console change the host mapping
e.g.
```
  "Hosts": {
    "dummy": "100.112.2.100",
  },
```
3. OSX dumps a black screen and reboots

**Version information:**
 - Device: laptop
 - OS: MacOS
 - OS version: 10.15.4
 - Tailscale version: 0.98

response.body:
Issue is with the --advertise-routes option. Eg: `tailscale up --advertise-routes=8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4`
I'm not sure if it's the documentation that's gone out of date here - [Connecting to external services with IP block lists via Tailscale](https://tailscale.com/kb/1059/ip-blocklist-relays?q=aws), or if the --advertise-routes option is supposed to be able to take individual IPs.

**Expected behavior**
IPs can be advertised, and not just CIDRs

**Current Behavior**
> $ "8.8.8.8" is not a valid CIDR prefix: invalid CIDR address: 8.8.8.8

response.title: How to re-authenticate in Linux
response.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

On Mac, there is a "Log Out" option, but on linux, following the official instructions, there is no easy way to figure out how to "log out"

I tried `sudo apt remove --purge tailscale` then reinstall, it still says "already authenticated, nothing to do"

Eventually I figured out I had to `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/tailscale`

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Be able to run command like so:

```
sudo tailscale up -h # find out what's there
sudo tailscale up -re-authenticate # prompt url to re-authenticate
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I tried remove + purge the package, the `/var/lib/tailscale/tailscaled.state` seems to be the file left behind that contains the keys and tokens.

commit.message:
wgengine/router: use inet.af/netaddr, not wgcfg.CIDR.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

response.body:
I think this is a good idea.

We are (I am ) going to have to produce a far more stripped-down wgcfg if we want to upstream it, so I think we'll end up using netaddr everywhere in our code and converting to whatever type wgcfg uses at the last moment just before reaching wireguard-go. So code like this should use netaddr.

Aside: reading this PR makes me wish the package were named ipaddr. `ipaddr.Prefix` would read a lot better than `netaddr.IPPrefix` and `ipaddr.IP` is harmless.

response.title: wgengine: wrap tun.Device to support filtering and packet injection.
response.body: As discussed with @crawshaw, right now, filtering and packet injection in wgengine depend on a patch to wireguard-go that probably isn't suitable for upstreaming. Namely, the following is part of the said patch (`device/device.go`): ```diff +type FilterResult int +const ( + FilterDrop FilterResult = iota + FilterAccept +) type Device struct { ... + filterLock sync.Mutex + filterIn func(b []byte) FilterResult + filterOut func(b []byte) FilterResult ... } ``` used as follows in `device/receive.go` (similar usage in `device/send.go`): ```diff func (device *Device) RoutineDecryption() { ... // after decryption, before writing the packet to the TUN + device.filterLock.Lock() + fp := device.filterIn + device.filterLock.Unlock() + if err == nil && fp != nil { + response := fp(elem.packet) + if response != FilterAccept { + err = FilteredErr + } + } ... ``` Additionally, `device/send.go` also adds `SendPacket`, duplicating a part of `RoutineReadFromTUN` to inject a packet by inserting it into the peer's nonce queue. The above need not be the case: `wireguard-go/tun.Device`, which `wireguar-go/device.Device` reads from, is an interface. For example, `wgengine/faketun.go` implements it to mock a TUN device for testing purposes. This patch implements the same interface to provide filtering and packet injection at the TUN device level, at which point the `wireguard-go` patch should no longer be necessary. --- This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/tailscale/tailscale/358)

This is not quite done yet (though all tests pass). I wanted to put it out now to make sure this is approximately what is expected. There are a few remaining points:

1. `wgtun` probably needs to be renamed, but I'm bad with names.
2. `SetFilter` from `userspace.go` should probably be brought into `wgtun/tun.go`. We no longer need to close over `userspaceEngine` in `filtin`, and this would allow us to remove the unsightly `Unwrap()` from `wgtun.Device`.

      This would make `wgtun.Device` less generic than it currently is, imposing a particular behavior on its filters. I think this is probably fine, as `wgtun` is intended to be "a TUN wrapper implementing the behavior `wgengine` wants" and not a reusable component. Part of the motivation here is to add DNS resolution more cleanly, which cannot be a pure filter (injects packets), and that (I think) would also be best placed in `wgtun`.
3. I'm observing drops of some weird packets, for example:
```
2020/05/07 10:28:30 Drop: Junk{} 48 junk!
  0000  60 00 00 00 00 08 3a ff  fe 80 00 00 00 00 00 00  `.....:.........
  0010  fb 57 1d ea 9c 39 8f b7  ff 02 00 00 00 00 00 00  .W...9..........
  0020  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 02  85 00 38 04 00 00 00 00  ..........8.....
```
None of these packets are IPv4 with destination in `100.64.0.0/10`, so I think they _should_ be dropped. The one above is actually an ICMPv6 Router Solicitation with `ipv6.dst == ff02::2`. I think the existing implementation just drops them in wireguard-go code before they reach the filter (`lookupPeer` happens earlier), but I thought this was worth verifying.
Thanks for the review! I'll squash commits when merging, but for now I want to keep the changes separate since the delta was kind of big.
With `(2)` above being done, I'm now sufficiently happy with this to remove the draft status.
I was going to run a performance test first, but now it seems like setting it up might still take a while. I addressed the feedback in the meantime to make this mergeable.

commit.message:
wgengine: wrap tun.Device to support filtering and packet injection.

Right now, filtering and packet injection in wgengine depend
on a patch to wireguard-go that probably isn't suitable for upstreaming.

This need not be the case: wireguard-go/tun.Device is an interface.
For example, faketun.go implements it to mock a TUN device for testing.

This patch implements the same interface to provide filtering
and packet injection at the tunnel device level,
at which point the wireguard-go patch should no longer be necessary.

Signed-off-by: Dmytro Shynkevych <dmytro@tailscale.com>

+	filter   *filter.Filter

commit.message:
Implement rate limiting on log messages

Addresses issue #317, where logs can get spammed with the same message
nonstop. Created a rate limiting closure on logging functions, which
limits the number of messages being logged per second based on format
string.

Signed-off-by: Wendi Yu <wendi.yu@yahoo.ca>

Replace time-dependent cache limiting with LRU

To keep memory usage as constant as possible, the previous cache
purging at periodic time intervals has been replaced by an LRU that
discards the oldest string when the capacity of the cache is reached.

Also fixed some formatting and commenting issues, and added better
testing for the rate limiter.

Signed-off-by: Wendi Yu <wendi.yu@yahoo.ca>

Remove unnecessary cache copying in ratelimiting

Signed-off-by: Wendi Yu <wendi.yu@yahoo.ca>

Use provided prefix function

Signed-off-by: Wendi Yu <wendi.yu@yahoo.ca>

Remove unnecessary ratelimiting in tests

Signed-off-by: Wendi Yu <wendi.yu@yahoo.ca>

response.body:
I think these two wrappers should be in the opposite order: rate limit it first, then add the Rusage prefix. Otherwise, the way RusagePrefixLog works, you'll have a separate rate limit for each possible Rusage value (which changes constantly).

You might also find it readable to just reuse the same variable name each time you add a wrapper:

logf := wgengine...
logf = logger...

There's probably not much need to rate limit the logs in tests. On the other hand, maybe we should have the test fail completely if the rate limiter ever kicks in during a test, which would seem to suggest a problem.
Or ("... original message: " + s) as the format string, and "args..." (including the ...) as the argument.

You probably want to use a fake Now() function for tests. To make that work, you need the rate limiter to accept a Now function at construction time (which in normal use is time.Now). Look at oss/control/controlcient/direct.go (and its use of a timeNow function) for an example.

Otherwise, this test could be unreliable if it runs slower than expected (like on a busy VM). Using a fake time function also lets you avoid using time.Sleep() in tests, which you should never do (if everyone did that, our tests would run much more slowly than they already do). You can instead have your fake timeNow function advance its timer, pretending to be 200ms in the future.

I don't think you actually want to use t.Logf() here. Instead, you want to write your own fake logger function that validates the input it was passed at different times. (The easiest way to do this is to define a logf local function that has access to variables from the test function, such as 't' and some variable that reflects whether you're expecting a message to be printed or not.)

This test doesn't call any function like t.Errorf() or t.Fatalf() here, so right now it can never fail. Your fake logf() function could call t.Fatalf() if the rate limiter tries to print at the "wrong" time.

This algorithm can work, but it leaves the struct at an unpredictable size: if more messages get printed per minute, we'll use more memory. It would be nice to have our memory usage be as stable as possible. You could look at this module for an LRU implementation instead: github.com/golang/groupcache/lru. 

An LRU has the disadvantage that items might be evicted from the cache if a lot of distinct format strings are used. On the other hand, that isn't the sort of bug we're defending against; if there are 100 messages that all need rate limiting, we're doomed anyway. An LRU would keep the most common format strings at the top of the list (least likely to get evicted), and the least common format strings at the bottom (most likely to be evicted, but doesn't matter because they don't need rate limiting because they're least common).

I was reading up on [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23229975/is-it-safe-to-remove-selected-keys-from-map-within-a-range-loop) about this, apparently in go when you call `delete` on a map entry it doesn't actually free up the memory for the garbage collector, it keeps all the data and just zombie flags it as "no longer in the map."
To make it actually available for the garbage collector you have to delete the map altogether, which is why I'm just copying over the values we still want to keep track of into a new map and setting the original to `nil` to be more clear about what I was doing - though I can just comment this in and clean up the code.
I might change how the purging is done entirely with the LRU Avery suggested though so this might go poof altogether :)

response.title: cmd/mkpkg: support adding empty directories.
response.body:
This eventually fixes #341, pending update to the packaging script.

As suggested in [this comment](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/341#issuecomment-622064118), it turns out that adding an empty directory at `/var/cache/tailscale` to the `%files` section of the rpm package fixes the issue (tested on a clean CentOS 8.1.1911 VM).

Since this may be useful for other directories in the future, this patch implements a generic way of adding empty directories to a package. In particular, it works for an empty list of empty directories, which is the default. This is not the case for `--files` and `--configs`, which always expect a nonempty list as an argument; hence the special treatment of `""` in `parseEmptyDirs`.

response.body:
To avoid unexpected behavior in strange edgecases, it might be advisable to be cautious and not perform MASQUERADING for traffic being sent 'into' the tailscale0 interface:
```suggestion
	if err := r.ipt4.Append("nat", "ts-postrouting", "!", "-o", r.tunname, "-m", "mark", "--mark", tailscaleSubnetRouteMark, "-j", "MASQUERADE"); err != nil {
```

Thanks for taking a look!

In the marking logic, we only mark packets that ingressed on tailscaled0 and are destined for a subnet route. So, we should be fine here.

Do you have a scenario in mind that trips this edge case? If we're going to add this, I'd like to leave a comment detailing an example, so that in 6 months we're not confused by the apparent non-necessity.

Correct, the marking logic should prevent this in most cases.

The (hypothetical and possibly unrealistic) case I had in mind is when we have a site-to-site setup with overlapping subnetworks announced at two locations.

I did run into this problem previously when building a network based on openvpn, and spent quite some time until I figured out that the packets were not actually dropped by my iptables rules but unexpectedly got a new source IP when routed into openvpn and that was why the traffic was not working as expected.

Let's assume we have relay node A being the HQ announcing the subnetwork 192.168.0.0/16.
Then branch office relay node B announcing 192.168.1.0/24.
And branch office relay node C announcing 192.168.2.0/24.
And C and B are unable to establish any connection between eachother (let's say due to some ongoing ISP peering issue).

Now a packet from 192.168.1.111 to 192.168.2.222 arrives at B, which sends it to A (as the 192.168.0.0/16 subnet points there).
At A, the packet is received and gets marked (as the 192.168.0.0/16 subnet route matches). Then it gets routed towards C (as on A, the 192.168.2.0/24 route exists and points there) and as it has the mark, it gets MASQUERADEd with the 100.64.X.Y IP of the tailscale0 interface.

Ah, I see. Yes, this breaks in the case where we "hairpin" traffic through a different Tailscale node. However, currently we do not permit this, and it likely breaks because of the prefix accept lists we configure at the wireguard layer.

I have to think about this. Your suggestion is good defensive programming, but I'm worried about adding defenses against problems we don't have yet, because then future-me has to figure out why I did that :).

I also accidentally pushes this PR into master just now, so I'm going to close this pull request, but I'm still thinking about this change.

response.body: We do this already on iOS. What's the motivation for doing it in CI?

We don't use these builds as release binaries, the actual build logic is in our non-OSS repository. We already use -trimpath for iOS builds, and I had a TODO to make it happen on other platforms too.

I don't think there's any need to do this in the OSS CI, since we don't use those binaries for anything. I'll port this into our corp build system and close the PR, if that works for you?

> We do this already on iOS. What's the motivation for doing it in CI?

As I mentioned in the last paragraph—unless I missed it—I don't think your own build scripts that generates binaries listed in https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/ is in this repo. So this was the only pertinent thing I managed to find and propose this change.  I don't think there's any material advantage to adding this for CI builds, so this can be just closed without merging but I think non-mobile platform builds can still use this.
Just added -trimpath to out corp repo's build logic. The next packages we build will have trimmed paths. Thanks for kicking this off!

response.body: Android O and later blocks the dup2 syscall, signal 31 (SIGSYS), code 1 (SYS_SECCOMP), fault addr -------- Cause: seccomp prevented call to disallowed x86_64 system call 33 so we need to use dup3 instead. Signed-off-by: Elias Naur --- This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/tailscale/tailscale/340)

response.title: Test flake: portlist_test.go:33: addProcesses: readdir: readdirent: no such file or directory
response.body: This error shows up in CI sometimes on Linux. Looks like the way we're using readdir() in /proc on Linux requires us to restart the readdir() operation if the dir changes. We're using this to read through a list of process fds, so if the process being scanned opens or closes a fd during our activity, we'll need to work around it to make this test flake go away.

response.title: iOS VPN backend crashes after a while
response.body:
We're investigating problems where the iOS VPN backend gets terminated by iOS after a while, either due to excess memory usage or excess CPU usage, or due to a Go panic. It seems to trigger more often when you hop between networks (eg. between wifi networks, or between wifi and LTE).

Bug #336 is a side effect of this.

response.title: iOS: incorrect message "No Internet Connection. Tailscale is paused while your device is offline."
response.body:
<!-- Please note, this template is for definite bugs, not requests for
support. If you need help with Tailscale, please email
support@tailscale.com. We don't provide support via Github issues. -->

**Describe the bug**
Tailscale loses connection after enough time in background, either killed or because of network changes. 

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Activate vpn through Tailscale
2. Don’t open app again for some indefinite long amount of time, say 1 day. 
3. Reopen app after seeing that vpn is no longer active.
4. See error: `No Internet Connection. Tailscale is paused while your device is offline. Please reconnect to the internet.`

**Expected behavior**
The vpn connection should always remain on.

**Screenshots**
After opening app again, this error is shown:

![IMG_0460](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/557509/80595497-5ba8f580-8a14-11ea-9451-f8d4f15b6356.PNG)

Then the vpn reconnects.

**Version information:**
 - Device: iPhone X
 - OS: iOS
 - OS version: 13.4.1
 - Tailscale version: 0.98.12

**Additional context**
There is an on-demand mode for vpn's in iOS, maybe tailscale can use it to remain always on - or at least have it an option.

> Why not force 8.8.8.8 and using the internal caching resolver, exactly the same on all platforms? I’m not excited to debug variable name caching behaviour across platforms anyway, and this goes double when the system resolver is sometimes also overridden (by us!) to be something that only works over tailscale.

8.8.8.8 may not be reachable. In some corporate networks, only the company resolvers are reachable on :53, to facilitate monitoring of DNS traffic.

Also, ignoring the local network's resolver results in HN coverage when Paul Vixie rants about you on IETF mailing lists :) https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/dnsop/WCVv57IizUSjNb2RQNP84fBclI0/

At least that would make the code run predictably across all platforms:
block our packets on your corp network, and Tailscale doesn't work.

But this module seems custom designed to be unpredictable:

1) It caches lookups for exactly 10 minutes, but (I think?) only on some
platforms, and doesn't refresh if you move between networks

2) It uses Go's resolver sometimes, and cgo sometimes, but the code to make
that decision is different from even the already-unpredictable Go default.
The current patch seems to add one more hack on top of that formula.

3) It uses a very half-hearted algorithm to avoid caching when on a captive
portal, but will happily cache for 10 minutes a wrong answer that
didn't match that half-hearted check, even if that cached answer failed to
actually retrieve an https page successfully.

And that leaves aside the separate problem that an *exactly* 10-minute
cache will eventually lead to thundering herds. Plus, because the cache is
on-demand rather than populated at startup, there'll be a race condition
between initializing the VPN settings and looking up hostnames. If you win
the race, you get 10 minutes of success, otherwise 10 minutes of failure?
What if we try to shut down the VPN during a Reauthenticate sequence (which
we do), will some other answer be cached? Will the cache happen to refresh
during the shutdown period?

This whole thing seems like it will be the cause of a lot of support
problems.

ᐧ

net/dnscache: don't use the Go resolver on Android

The local resolver is not available for apps on Android.

Signed-off-by: Elias Naur <mail@eliasnaur.com>

response.body:
Well, I added a system-wide DNS caching proxy to Android in 2011: https://github.com/aosp-mirror/platform_bionic/commit/0ec85334ff375a2b7823f322e083d4a0ea24c289 ... so each app doesn't need to do its own DNS + caching. (It just doesn't speak the normal DNS protocol that Go can speak)

I assume it or something like it is still there. But if we just do libc calls to `getaddrinfo` etc, Android's libc should do the right thing and cache the results.

But it's not like our iOS comment above is totally accurate, either, so.... *shrug*

You can submit, or fix both comments and submit. Your call.

What I got before this change was a bunch of "connection refused" on UDP port 53:

```04-27 18:18:23.772 29228 29262 I gio     : 2020/04/27 18:18:23 derphttp.Client.Recv: connecting to https://derp4.tailscale.com/derp

```

so I assumed that there wasn't a local resolver. How about

"No accessible local resolver on Android."?
I changed it to "The local resolver is not available on Android."

response.title: Auto-added iptables rules on Linux refer to eth0 and are otherwise nonsense
response.body:
The way we add iptables forwarding rules on Linux was an old hack that works for approximately nobody, except by coincidence.

Bugs:

- [x] Refers specifically to an interface named "eth0" which is very uncommon on modern Linux systems.
- [x] Get re-added (but never deleted) every time the app starts
- [x] Creates a wildcard MASQUERADE rule rather than tight settings that do exactly what we need
- [x] Does not refer specifically to the network interface name obtained from the 'tun' object
- [x] Does not block incoming 100.x packets from arriving on non-tailscale interfaces (a potential avenue for attack)
- [x] Hard to clean up: should use an iptables sub-table(s) for our special rules, so that we can flush-then-add the rules whenever we want, and a single rule in each toplevel table that refers to the sub-table.
- [x] Doesn't take precedence: the toplevel reference rule should be added with -I 1 instead of -A, so it can be preferred over other rules, and so it is easy to delete even when upgrading between versions, because it will never be any different
- [x] Doesn't notice when something else in the system mangles or inserts itself in front of the rules: should forcibly re-add itself at the top of the toplevel tables occasionally
- [x] Doesn't set rp_filter correctly automatically
- [x] Doesn't set /proc/sys/net/ip_forward automatically

- [x] Futzing with the firewall should be possible to completely disable if desired.

As a result, we have to provide firewall setup instructions in https://tailscale.com/kb/1019/install-subnets.

The good news is that because of the hardcoded eth0, at least the rules do not themselves create any major security issues.

response.title: Toggling DisableDERP leaves nodes in an invalid state
response.body:
Steps:
- Start a Windows node with DisableDERP=True at startup. You can do this by previously starting the node, disabling DERP using the UI, and then exit + restarting.
  - Note that it registers with tailcontrol *without* mentioning a DERP server.
- Enable DERP using the UI
  - Note that it does *not* re-register with tailcontrol; the node still has no DERP server associated.
- Try to contact a node behind a firewall
  - DERP is enabled locally, so it tries to connect to that node using DERP
  - The remote node receives the connection but cannot reply via DERP since the other node has no registered DERP server.

In general, toggling the DisableDERP pref at runtime seems very untested.

04-23,14:36:03.590 63.0M/92.1M [ICORl] - Failed to send data packet too many DERP packets queued; dropping

If you're dropping packets, printing a log message per dropped packets is obviously excessive.

04-23,14:36:38.813 srv: 93.4M/0.0M ConsumeMessageInitiation: could not find peer by public key: ...
04-23,14:36:38.813 srv: 93.4M/0.0M Received invalid initiation message from ...
04-23,14:36:38.959 srv: 93.5M/0.0M ConsumeMessageInitiation: could not find peer by public key: ...
04-23,14:36:38.959 srv: 93.5M/0.0M Received invalid initiation message from ...
04-23,14:36:39.014 srv: 93.5M/0.0M ConsumeMessageInitiation: could not find peer by public key: ...

First of all, it would be nice if this were one line instead of two. But second, if we're getting invalid handshakes, we have to rate limit them, because a DDoS attack could make this much worse.

More generally, it would be really nice to just globally rate limit each message format string to keep it from getting out of control. If we do that, of course we also need to print a message clearly indicating that excess messages were suppressed.

response.title: Support for CentOS 6
response.body:
CentOS 6 is still supported, in the "maintenance updates only" phase of life according to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CentOS#End-of-support_schedule . It EOLs in 6 months.

We don't ship Tailscale packages for CentOS 6 for a couple of reasons:
 - It doesn't run systemd, so we'd have to write and support legacy sysvinit scripts, and reimplement missing functionality like automatic restarts. CentOS 6 is the only distro in our current list that would need this.
 - It's missing policy routing features that we require to avoid routing loops (#144). (This is not implemented yet, but fixes a high-priority bug on linux)

In other words, CentOS 6 would be a special singleton compared to other distros we support. Given that it's reaching EOL in 6 months, it doesn't seem worth supporting at this point. This issue exists as something we can point to, and track whether to revisit this choice.

response.title: FR: Implement peer MTU discovery through the tailnet
response.body:
Bug #246 and others note that we have a hardcoded MTU calculation on different OSes, either using a strictly fixed size or some formula based on the MTU of the default route's interface. This is also more or less what plain wireguard does.

Unfortunately it's guaranteed to be completely wrong on some networks. The MTU can be constrained by either end of a link. If WireGuard packets are using the DF flag, then intermediate routers will refuse to fragment them and will (attempt to) send back an ICMP Fragmentation Needed packet. WireGuard doesn't trust those because they could be forged, so it discards them instead.

A proper fix would do a more expensive form of MTU probing in both directions, which neither relies on nor trusts ICMP Fragmentation Needed packets. We can afford to try harder than regular TCP would do, because we can calculate the MTU once per long-lived peer connection instead of once per short-lived TCP connection.

Once we know the MTU, we'd have to generate our own synthetic ICMP Fragmentation Needed packets inside the tunnel, so that the inner TCP can do proper PMTU discovery.

response.title: systemd unit prints benign warnings on CentOS 7
response.body: CentOS 7 uses systemd 219, 5.5 years old. It doesn't understand the following config directives, and prints warnings about our use of them: ``` [Unit] StartLimitInterval= StartLimitBurst= [Service] StateDirectory= StateDirectoryMode= CacheDirectory= CacheDirectoryMode= ``` These were introduced in systemd 229 and 235, 3.5 years ago. The warnings are fairly benign. The restart limiters means systemd might stop tailscaled if it goes into a tight crashloop (whereas we want it to keep retrying for ever), and the missing *Directory statements are just about pre-creating some directories and setting permissions on them - but tailscaled can take care of that itself too. The only way to shut up these warnings without losing the functionality on more modern OSes is to start building packages that are customized for every distro, as opposed to our current sneaky trick of using a single .deb/.rpm for all distros. That's a lot of work to shut up a couple of cosmetic warts, so I think the high effort/small benefit makes this low priority. [Front conversations](https://app.frontapp.com/open/top_38olt)

response.title: Dry-run support for testing --authkey
response.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

In order to test #270 with CI tests, I created a new Tailscale account and use an auth key from that account for all of my tests. I would love to be able to test Tailscale against this account without generating "real" machines that I need to manually go in and clean up later.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Something like Let's Encrypt's [staging environment](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/staging-environment/) would be great. Some CLI flag like `--dry-run` that lets me test creating machines against my Tailscale account to validate whether I've configured my server/device/authentication correctly without actually generating those servers in my account.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

This is a pretty low priority request. As people incorporate Tailscale into their environments, the ability to "test" their setup without registering their server could be beneficial, however.

**Additional context**

Tailscale is :tada: , thanks for your work to put together this product.

response.title: Wake-on-LAN packet support
response.body:
I often need to SSH to my Mac at home, but sometimes it's asleep.

But I have other tailscaled nodes on my network that don't sleep.

It'd be nice if we could transparently send Wake-on-LAN packets automatically.

Imagine three nodes:

* Laptop at coffee shop
* macOS desktop at home
* Linux server at home (Synology NAS, etc)

When I run "ssh bradfitz@100.x.y.z", my laptop's tailscaled could know that the macOS desktop hasn't been seen in a while, and send a DERP message to the Linux server at home to do the Wake-on-LAN packet to the macOS's MAC address.

And/or it could be more explicit, too, like `tailscale wake <node_name>` which would then print out status and optionally block until the node is woken up and responding via Tailscale.

/cc @danderson @crawshaw @apenwarr

response.title: T-Mobile LTE breaks tailscale connectivity due to CGNAT and/or IPv6-only
response.body:
Sorry for the rough title, there's layers here.

TMobile's IPV6 implementation is breaking SSH down the tailscale provided tunnel. After finding a client that exposed some connection logs, I noted that I was being provided a v6 address to connect to, regardless of if I was using my tailscale IP directly or an A record pointing to the tailscale IP.

Interestingly, HTTP(s) requests via Chrome iOS to the same host were working.

I was able to work around this by applying a device profile (for testing) which allows for ipv4/ipv6 rather than v6 only, but, if possible, the iOS client application should attempt to navigate this network.

**To Reproduce**
iPhone on T-Mobile, connected to LTE.
Tailscale tunnel active.
SSH to CentOS7 host via tailscale IP

**Version information:**
 - Device: iPhone 11 Pro Max

 - OS version: 13.3.1
 - Tailscale version: 0.97.78

response.body: ping @bradfitz @danderson
I think @danderson is better qualified to review this one.

This is generally good, however a couple of things are going to make me decline this PR:
 - This really needs to live in our non-OSS CI, which is where the rest of releases gets built. Due to weirdness in our repo structure, that's the only way to burn correct version numbers into the binary at this time.
 - Pushing Docker images signals that we support running Tailscale in a Docker image. However, early adopters who've tried have discovered a lot of ways in which this falls apart (most recently: broken iptables interactions between host and container), because we currently do not support this and haven't done the legwork to debug running as a container. I would prefer to order things the other way around: make our docker image more robust, _then_ start pushing it automatically.

@bradfitz thoughts on the above?

I agree on the second bullet completely.

I'm less convinced that this needs to be closed long-term, though. The version number weirdness we could solve somehow. But maybe we'll have a plan for that by the time we support Docker/Kubernetes well.

Those are good points, and I wasn't aware of the issues on containerized version.
 
And quite frankly doing release automation can vary for each project/team and I wasn't sure how heavily the other closed CI system is being used.

Regardless I'm open to give a hand on both if need be, let me know.

If you want to avoid the perception of supported container images, but still have builds available, why not create a `tailscale/tailscale-git` repository and build every commit? Because nothing would be tagged as a release, it'd be clearer that they are developer builds and you'd get a form of "CI" that tests the Dockerfile for every commit.

This is what I've done in the past, then I only curate and promote releases to the canonical container repository (e.g. `tailscale/tailscale`).

This is on hold for #504. We want to make our Dockerfile a bit more usable before we start getting too many bug reports about it.

Also, we'd want to do this in our corp meta repo probably.

I'm going to close this for now but we'll revisit it soonish I hope.

response.body:
The reason I dropped `v` from Docker tag was because anything after `:` is considered some sort of a _version_ and notion of `v` in that was kind of redundant. There are so many cases of both sides out there, two very notable ones:

- Grafana [tags](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/tags) with leading `v` BUT [images](https://hub.docker.com/r/grafana/grafana/tags) without.
- Prometheus [tags](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tags) with leading `v` AND [images](https://hub.docker.com/r/prom/prometheus/tags) also with.

At the end, this was a personal preference. And to be clear I'm not affiliated with Tailscale and this PR is only a personal contribution.

response.title: Tailscale and k3s don't play nice together
response.body:
Tracking bug to figure out teething issues with running k3s and tailscale together, using Tailscale to provide a secure inter-node mesh for Kubernetes traffic.

Setup: bring up a k3s cluster on Ubuntu, with one controller and a couple of nodes. Install tailscale on all of them, and edit k3s's systemd unit to add `--flannel-iface tailscale0` to all nodes. This'll make k3s use the Tailscale mesh for inter-node traffic, which is swanky.

Probably need to adjust MTUs on tailscale0, k3s does vxlan which doesn't play well with our default MTU settings.

Main problem is that restarting tailscaled breaks the k3s overlay network. My suspicion is that flannel doesn't like it when tailscale0 vanishes then comes back, and doesn't correctly restore routes it had configured - but I have no proof.

In the other direction, restarting k3s seems to make tailscaled spin and consume all the CPU, for reasons not obvious. May be worse on 0.97-45 than on the latest unstable, but we have reports of it happening with both versions.

net/peers: helpers for peer lookups

as an os.Exec call using tailscale status command. In the future, it
would be great to use a better method.

response.body:
This style of defining an interface just to return it isn't really idiomatic Go. Generally you define an interface for something you accept.

This is a lot of indirection for something that could just be `func GetPeers() ([]Peer, error)`, no?

Or if there are plans for more extensibility, using a concrete type would give you places to add optional knobs in the future (so returning a `*Queryer` instead, at which point you can drop the constructor and just document that the Querier zero value is valid).

response.title: Easy unattended installations, for example with Ansible
response.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I would like to have unattended installations of Tailscale, which don't seem possible at the moment.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Currently, the last step for installing and starting Tailscale is to run `tailscale up`. This command blocks until the URL presented in the shell is visited. This makes unattended installations, for example bringing up multiple clients from an Ansible play, difficult. It would be nice to have a form of command that would automatically register the client with the server:

`tailscale up <unique-server-url>`

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Clearly, security is a concern. Perhaps a separate url could be pre-generated on the admin console for each new client ahead of installing them? Or the server url would only be valid for hosts with a particular name?

Another possibility would be to make the process more asynchronous by outputting the current text, but backgrounding the process that waits for the registration. (I'm assuming here that Ansible would then return the text as stdout and I could parse it for the URL.)

**Additional context**

I think that just about covers it.

response.title: DNS setup (on Linux)
response.body:
Currently, it does not seem as if Linux hosts pick up the DNS config from the admin panel when connecting to tailscale.

I guess this is because it is disabled in the code (`TODO`):
https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/a7e7c7b548dd7903326360b4d9740a0412779433/wgengine/router_linux.go#L155-L159

Looking at what it would attempt if enabled, it seems as if tailscale **replaces `/etc/resolv.conf`** with it's own version.

Wouldn't that cause issues with other files modifying `resolv.conf` as well? It might be a better idea to use `resolvconf` if available (https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/Openresolv), like `dhcpd` does and only fallback to hard replacing?

response.title: Excessive tailscale logging in system log
response.body:
Report from a friend, as well as a couple of users: tailscaled is the single most verbose thing in their system logs, by a very long way. This is a problem for them because they do centralized logs collection, and so extremely verbose tailscaled logs multiplied by many machines depletes the central logstore's disk space at alarming rates.

We've heard this from several quarters, and our general plan for this is "do less stuff, because this will generate less logs". Filing this bug (a) to track that and (b) to decide whether that's enough. Even with things like eager handshaking disabled, we're still likely to log a _lot_ more than the rest of the system combined, because we intend these logs to be debug-level stuff.

Unfortunately we don't use log levels, so it's not a simple matter of "lower the syslog spamminess and only push debug logs into logtail". Unless we add some kind of log levels, our only option is to turn off syslog output entirely.

response.body: **Describe the bug** DNS servers configured in the admin panel don't seem to be picked up by (MacOS / iOS) clients. **To Reproduce** Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. response.title: wgengine: remove IpcSetOperation on LinkChange
response.body: This was only done occasionally, but was extremely disruptive when done and is no longer necessary. It used to be that when switching links, we had to immediately generate handshakes to everyone we were communicating with to punch a hole in any NAT we were talking through. (This ended up not really working, because in the process we got rid of our session keys and ended up having a futile conversation for many seconds.) Now we have DERP, our link change propogates to the other side as a new list of endpoints, so they start spraying packets. We will definitely get one thanks to DERP, which will cause us to spray, opening any NAT we are behind. The result is that for good connections, we don't trash session keys and cause an interruption. Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw --- This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/tailscale/tailscale/279)

commit.message:
wgengine: remove IpcSetOperation on LinkChange

This was only done occasionally, but was extremely disruptive
when done and is no longer necessary.

It used to be that when switching links, we had to immediately
generate handshakes to everyone we were communicating with to
punch a hole in any NAT we were talking through. (This ended up
not really working, because in the process we got rid of our
session keys and ended up having a futile conversation for many
seconds.)

Now we have DERP, our link change propogates to the other side
as a new list of endpoints, so they start spraying packets.
We will definitely get one thanks to DERP, which will cause us
to spray, opening any NAT we are behind.

The result is that for good connections, we don't trash session
keys and cause an interruption.

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

response.body:
@bradfitz this fix does what readFrame's comment claims it should have already been doing [1]. The framing won't be off because of that `io.CopyN(ioutil.Discard, ...)` call.

[1]

```
129 // If the frame is less than maxSize but greater than len(b), len(b)
130 // bytes are read, err will be io.ErrShortBuffer, and frameLen and t
131 // will both be set. That is, callers need to explicitly handle when
132 // they get more data than expected.
```

The client side is already aware of this possibility. For example, `recvServerKey()` tries to be "future-proof" (but it would just crash without this fix).

```
 60 func (c *Client) recvServerKey() error {
 61     var buf [40]byte
 62     t, flen, err := readFrame(c.br, 1<<10, buf[:])
 63     if err == io.ErrShortBuffer {
 64         // For future-proofing, allow server to send more in its greeting.
 65         err = nil
 66     }
```
Ah, okay. I'll take another look at this later. It might be tomorrow until I get back to this.

This doesn't seem right. The caller would get a truncated result and the framing would be off for all future reads.

If anything I'd just detect this and return an error to the caller which should ultimately break the connection forever, since it's unusable at that point anyway (frame header was already read).

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style

+
+// Package logheap logs a heap pprof profile.
+package logheap
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"io"
+	"os"
+	"runtime"
+	"runtime/pprof"
+	"time"
+)
+
+// LogHeap writes a JSON logtail record with the base64 heap pprof to
+// os.Stderr.
+func LogHeap() {
+	logHeap(os.Stderr)
+}
+
+type logTail struct {
+	ClientTime string `json:"client_time"`
+}
+
+type pprofRec struct {
+	Heap []byte `json:"heap,omitempty"`
+}
+
+type logLine struct {
+	LogTail logTail  `json:"logtail"`
+	Pprof   pprofRec `json:"pprof"`
+}
+
+func logHeap(w io.Writer) error {
+	runtime.GC()
+	buf := new(bytes.Buffer)
+	pprof.WriteHeapProfile(buf)
+	return json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(logLine{
+		LogTail: logTail{ClientTime: time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)},
+		Pprof:   pprofRec{Heap: buf.Bytes()},
+	})
+}

+func TestLogHeap(t *testing.T) {
+	var buf bytes.Buffer
+	if err := logHeap(&buf); err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	t.Logf("Got line: %s", buf.Bytes())
+
+	var ll logLine
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(buf.Bytes(), &ll); err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+
+	zr, err := gzip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(ll.Pprof.Heap))
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}

+	if err != nil {

+	}
+	// Just sanity check it. Too lazy to properly decode the protobuf. But see that

+		t.Errorf("raw proto didn't contain `alloc_objects`: %q", rawProto)

commit.message:
RFC, derp/derphttp: Avoid redundand reconnects.

1. closeForReconnect() may be closing already reestablished
connections. In the worst case, Send() and Recv(), running in
concurrent loops, would be running connect() and closeForReconnect()
calls in lockstep endlessly.
2. Reconnecting doesn't seem to make sense for non-networking errors
(or at least not for all). e.g. derphttp.Client.Send() may fail
with "packet too big", which is a local issue.

Signed-off-by: Dmitry Adamushko <da@stablebits.net>

response.body: derp.Client methods could also return something like `ErrUnusableTransport` to indicate cases that require reconnecting (as opposed to cases when the current transport remains usable). The use of raw networking errors here is insufficient. Perhaps the error handling case should be addressed separately.

response.title: derp/derp_server: unregisterClient() for replaced client connections.

This changes the locking rules of the `sentTo` field but doesn't update the docs.

Update the docs?

Also, `Server.Close()` may miss some clients without this [1]. OK to include into the same commit (as a rather minor thing)?

[1]
```
diff --git a/derp/derp_server.go b/derp/derp_server.go
index 1f866ad..4596762 100644
--- a/derp/derp_server.go
+++ b/derp/derp_server.go
@@ -153,6 +153,10 @@ func (s *Server) Accept(nc Conn, brw *bufio.ReadWriter, remoteAddr string) {
        closed := make(chan struct{})
 
        s.mu.Lock()
+       if s.closed {
+               s.mu.Unlock()
+               return
+       }
        s.accepts.Add(1)             // while holding s.mu for connNum read on next line
        connNum := s.accepts.Value() // expvar sadly doesn't return new value on Add(1)
        s.netConns[nc] = closed

> Also, Server.Close() may miss some clients without this 

The server is never really closed, and if it is closed, all the clients will lose their routes anyway, so it doesn't really affect anything.

You can send it in a separate change if you'd like, though.

> Excellent idea, but is the global map worth it? You can define a type TZs sync.Map and let the caller manage storing the map.

I'm having a hard time imagining when that would be better off. If you make the map in some client struct you can manage the lifetime and get back down to zero, but you can also end up caching more overall. And at the cost of a worse API. And the worst case global cache size is ~8KB if all 24*3 zones are cached. (3=we only cache :00, :15, :30 offsets from the hour)

Let's wait on that until we have a use. I'd prefer the simpler API for now.

commit.message:
tstime: add new package for time utilities, starting with Parse3339

Go's time.Parse always allocates a FixedZone for time strings not in
UTC (ending in "Z"). This avoids that allocation, at the cost of
adding a cache.

response.title: [wip] apputils: authenticate net/http and grpc requests with Tailscale
response.body: Adding a small apputils package to authenticate incoming net/http and gRPC requests by checking if they were sent through the Tailscale network. This would primarily be used for admin panels, and other internal services which may be run on publicly accessible servers, but should only be accessed by employees / people on your internal network. This was initially inspired by https://twitter.com/apenwarr/status/1245718870150778880. A few design decisions that it would be great to get your feedback on: - Chose the `apputils` package name since I foresee additional application-level functions being added in the future, perhaps in the context of distributed systems / logging / security. Open to ideas here. - Named the two functions `AuthenticateHTTP` and `AuthenticateGRPC`, though this may be a little misleading. Again, open to ideas. - Currently basing authentication on the cmd/tsshd implementation. Are there any other checks we should be doing other than ensuring the remote address is a Tailscale IP? - My goal was to authenticate gRPC requests without importing "google.golang.org/grpc/peer" (which has a rather large dependency tree), but I was unsuccessful. --- This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/tailscale/tailscale/259)

response.body:
Sorry, I think this is what @apenwarr was saying we should **not** be doing. This is purely checking if the IP is in the CGNAT range. That's not enough. 

Also, I'm wary of pulling in all of grpc and protobuf for this util func.

This probably needs to be split up a bit.

Ahh, I must have misunderstood what he was trying to say, my apologies. What other checks are necessary in order to properly authenticate an incoming request? If these are something that I could work on, I'd be happy to do so.

As per splitting up the PR, I do agree this would probably be a good idea. I'd like to spend some more time on authenticating gRPC requests without pulling in all of gRPC/Protobuf, so perhaps we can add a TODO item here and remove any mention of gRPC from this PR.

The concern is that `interfaces.IsTailscaleIP` isn't quite strong enough for this use case. Note that its docs (https://godoc.org/tailscale.com/net/interfaces#IsTailscaleIP) don't say that it's necessarily a Tailscale IP, and that Tailscale is running locally, etc.

Some mobile phones in Europe at least get an IPv4 over DHCP/etc in the same range. We wouldn't want two of those customers hitting each other's phones/tethered laptops and getting access. It's a bit contrived, but for an authorization function it should probably be pretty paranoid & accurate.

Note in our proof-of-concept SSH server, we wait for the tailscale interface to appear and then listen on its IP directly: https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/master/cmd/tsshd/tsshd.go#L59 ... that's a bit more paranoid. (it could be stricter, though)

To make this PR stronger, I'd also check that a Tailscale interface exists with an address in the same range.

I appreciate you getting back to me! I will take some time to fix up this PR.

Random question, Is there a way to get some sort of network map of a users internal Tailscale network? (e.g. a list of all hostname/ip pairs that are apart of their account?). I think this would be especially useful in the context of building distributed systems (peer discovery type of applications), and for security applications. If not, I'd appreciate if you could point me to some documentation and/or code around looking up the current registry of assigned Tailscale interfaces (more in the context of this PR - checking if a Tailscale interface exists with address in same range as incoming request remote address).
See `tailscale status` in recent versions.

Oh this is amazing... is there some way that I can get this data programmatically (eg. from some existing code in this repository) rather than having to issue os.Exec calls (which I'm not sure would work on all platforms?)

The ultimate security check for an incoming request would check to see if an incoming request is coming from a users ipn (inter-planetary network? :smile:), and that they are listening on their Tailscale interface.
We don't have an exactly stable API yet, but in the meantime os/exec should work everywhere. I assume you saw the `--json` output mode too?
Closing this PR and splitting up into smaller, more defined CLs. Will reference our conversation here in those.

@@ -220,3 +226,48 @@ func (p *Policy) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error {
 	}
 	return nil
 }
+
+// newLogtailTransport returns the HTTP Transport we use for uploading logs.
+func newLogtailTransport() *http.Transport {
+	// Start with a copy of http.DefaultTransport and tweak it a bit.
+	tr := http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone()
+
+	// We do our own zstd compression on uploads, and responses never contain any payload,
+	// so don't send "Accept-Encoding: gzip" to save a few bytes on the wire, since there
+	// will never be any body to decompress:
+	tr.DisableCompression = true
+
+	// Log whenever we dial:
+	tr.DialContext = func(ctx context.Context, netw, addr string) (net.Conn, error) {
+		nd := &net.Dialer{
+			Timeout:   30 * time.Second,
+			KeepAlive: 30 * time.Second,
+			DualStack: true,
+		}
+		t0 := time.Now()
+		c, err := nd.DialContext(ctx, netw, addr)
+		d := time.Since(t0).Round(time.Millisecond)
+		if err != nil {
+			log.Printf("logtail: dial %q failed: %v (in %v)", addr, err, d)
+		} else {
+			log.Printf("logtail: dialed %q in %v", addr, d)
+		}
+		return c, err
+	}
+
+	// We're contacting exactly 1 hostname, so the default's 100
+	// max idle conns is very high for our needs. Even 2 is
+	// probably double what we need:
+	tr.MaxIdleConns = 2
+
+	// Provide knob to force HTTP/1 for log uploads.
+	// TODO(bradfitz): remove this debug knob once we've decided
+	// to upload via HTTP/1 or HTTP/2 (probably HTTP/1). Or we might just enforce
+	// it server-side.
+	if h1, _ := strconv.ParseBool(os.Getenv("TS_DEBUG_FORCE_H1_LOGS")); h1 {
+		tr.TLSClientConfig = nil // DefaultTransport's was already initialized w/ h2
+		tr.ForceAttemptHTTP2 = false
+		tr.TLSNextProto = map[string]func(authority string, c *tls.Conn) http.RoundTripper{}
+	}
+	return tr
+}

response.title: tailscale0 MTU set incorrectly on GCP
response.body:
tailscale0 MTU seems to be set at a static 1420 bytes. This works fine on clouds that give customers 1500 bytes of MTU, but GCP only gives customers 1460 bytes. So, pings work, but anything more hefty (e.g. SSH) either times out, or takes an eternity to function.

Fixing is a bit tricky, since by definition we don't quite know which path we might be using to peer with people. We could set an ultra conservative 1280b everywhere, but blerg. We could set min(mtus)-wireguard_overhead. Or we could handle PMTU discovery and packet fragmentation in tailscaled.

cc @bradfitz @crawshaw

response.title: MIPS packages/binaries
response.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Not a problem, but some network gear like Unifi is MIPS based:

```
admin@ubnt:~$ uname -a
Linux ubnt 3.10.107-UBNT #1 SMP Fri May 17 16:26:51 UTC 2019 mips64 GNU/Linux
```
It might be desirable to run tailscale on perhaps your router, and then do forwarding that wat

**Describe the solution you'd like**


Ideally I'd to see the packages/binaries built with goreleaser, so adding new architectures isn't hard! I managed to successfully build a binary with go build that worked as needed on a MIPS device pretty easily though:

```
GOOS=linux GOARCH=mips GOMIPS=softfloat go build -o /tmp/tailscale ./cmd/...
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Buying different network hardware? Seems like overkill ;-)

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+// Package policy contains various policy decisions that need to be
+// shared between the node client & control server.
+package policy
+
+import "tailscale.com/tailcfg"
+
+// IsInterestingService reports whether service s on the given operating
+// system (a version.OS value) is an interesting enough port to report
+// to our peer nodes for discovery purposes.
+func IsInterestingService(s tailcfg.Service, os string) bool {
+	if s.Proto != tailcfg.TCP {
+		return false
+	}
+	if os != "windows" {
+		// For non-Windows machines, assume all TCP listeners
+		// are interesting enough. We don't see listener spam
+		// there.
+		return true
+	}
+	// Windows has tons of TCP listeners. We need to move to a blacklist
+	// model later, but for now we just whitelist some common ones:
+	switch s.Port {
+	case 22, // ssh
+		80,    // http
+		443,   // https (but no hostname, so little useless)
+		3389,  // rdp
+		5900,  // vnc
+		32400, // plex
+
+		// And now some arbitary HTTP dev server ports:
+		// Eventually we'll remove this and make all ports
+		// work, once we nicely filter away noisy system
+		// ports.
+		8000, 8080, 8443, 8888:
+		return true
+	}
+	return false
+}

commit.message:
ipn, ipn/policy: filter portlist to a short list of "interesting" ports

Adds new package ipn/policy to be shared between node client & control server.

Signed-off-by: Brad Fitzpatrick <bradfitz@tailscale.com>

response.body:
But as @crawshaw I think said earlier, once we have something like this "is interesting" function, we can then share it both with the reporting side, and control, so control can filter things upon report (for old clients) and send fewer diffs even for the old clients.

So this should move to the portlist package probably.
@apenwarr, PTAL. I tried to strike a compromise by only doing the whitelist on Windows for now. That's the only place where we see the port spam noise.
Once this is in, I'll use this new func from the server to filter out Windows ports from old clients.
Turns out the ipn package is a huge dep to add to control. Moved it to a new ipn/policy package instead.
I'm reasonably sure I'm going to regret the lack of filtering on non-windows platforms, but not as much as I'll regret leaving it as is, so ok for now. :)

> I'm reasonably sure I'm going to regret the lack of filtering on non-windows platforms

We can always change it later. Looking at the data, though, only Windows seems to be terrible in this regard.

I don't think this wildcard will work reliably. It still means 1/64th of randomly generated port numbers will generate service map updates, which on a machine with lots of churn (Chrome and/or Windows, yay) could still be a problem. I also wouldn't feel confident offering "just any port starting with 8" as an http:// link by default in a UI, since it might be a random Chrome listener, so the long list doesn't help us build the user-facing product AFAICS.

In the future we could have a CLI or GUI for exporting ports (bonus points: let the user actually describe the service being offered), and/or probe them to make sure they're valid http/https before publishing. In the meantime, I'd be more comfortable having a very short list of auto-published ports and documentation that says basically "if you want your http server to show up, run it on 80, 443 or 8080."

(I guess 443 won't even work right since we don't know what hostname to use)

If we just want the full port list available for debugging, I suggest just printing a log line with all the numbers whenever portlist gives a new list. That won't cause any tailcontrol churn.

It's easier to add more ports in the future than to take them away.

Yeah, I also wasn't super keen on adding policy to the portlist package. Policy in ipn SGTM. Will move.

I agree we should probe new ports when they come into existence and see what they are before reporting them to tailcontrol.

I'm still with @crawshaw on not liking the whitelist in general. We _can_ document that 8080 is magic, but it kills the magic of it just working for whatever port you're using. I suppose we can do that later, though.

Sure, will restrict to 8080 for now. At least it'll motivate me to do a better thing sooner.

Ok, good.

I'm not kidding about the log lines; it won't be too spammy to do (iOS, the battery sensitive one, has basically no visible listeners to our sandbox, and certainly not ones that change a lot) and then you'll have all the information you ever needed to tune the magic however you want.

Do random ports really get assigned in 8000-9000?

According to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemeral_port, there's well-defined behavior on various OSs. The Linux kernel assigns ephemeral ports from a declared range:

```
$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range
32768	60999
```

It looks like Windows Server 2008 might use ports in the [8000,8999] range but nothing else does.

Logs would be very useful here to let us tune this later on, especially if the logs give us a sense of how long-lived ports are. (I suspect there's an interesting category of short-lived ports that keep coming back, i.e. my compile-run loop bash command has the same port number each time.)

Re: moving it to the portlist package, philosophically I feel like the portlist package is just a utility that shouldn't have opinions on what is interesting. The ipn package is where I tried to put the "product opinions" so far (eg. the mess that is ipn.Prefs). But I don't really care, and that would be an easy way to share it.

commit.message:
ipn: filter portlist to a short list of "interesting" ports.

Uploading a list of all listeners turned out to be hopelessly naive.
Windows has zillions of them under normal use (yikes, but that's
another story), and Chrome creates and destroys them constantly,
possibly related to webrtc.

Instead, we'll only return a list of the ports that we expect to expose
in the UI within the near future.

Signed-off-by: Avery Pennarun <apenwarr@tailscale.com>

response.body:
Happy to not export it.

We can do better later. The whitelist has two advantages right now:

1) It dramatically reduces useless service list updates to tailcontrol,
which are the cause of almost all updates

2) It will let us build a dumb-but-easy UI like "run this program to launch
a remote desktop" or "run this program to launch ssh" for nodes that have
those servers.

It's better than simply disabling the portlist because we'll be able to add
the UI without waiting for a rollout of new software to all the nodes in a
domain. I definitely don't claim this is the end-all right solution, but
it'll let us get some glitz into the GUIs quickly while removing one or our
most urgent scaling problems.
