response.title: Can't resolve names after connecting on macOS
response.body:
**Describe the bug**
After connecting Tailscale on macOS, I can ping and connect to other nodes by IP but all DNS resolutions stopped working.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Connect tailscale
2. Try to open any website
3. DNS fail

**Expected behavior**
I expect my local resolver to still be used instead of forcing to use Tailscale's.

**Screenshots**

Output of `scutil --dns` after connecting:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10713/77820352-f0e95f00-70e1-11ea-84cc-f29dbbb217d4.png)

The `100.90.7.1` doesn't resolve any name.

**Version information:**
 - Device: MacBook Pro 15 ice 2016 
 - OS: MacOS
 - OS version: 10.15.4
 - Tailscale version: 0.97.78 from App Store 

**Additional context**
First time trying Tailscale. No DNS settings in admin. As I said above, connectivity on the IP level is working fine.

response.title: CentOS 8 Installation - Missing "iptables" command
response.body:
**Describe the bug**
When installing Tailscale on a new CentOS 8 machine (following the [website docs](https://tailscale.com/kb/1051/install-centos-8)), if `iptables` isn't installed, `tailscaled` will enter an infinite systemd restart loop. This occurred when configuring a reverse proxy instance via DigitalOcean, who doesn't install `iptables` with the default CentOS 8.1 image.


**To Reproduce**
1. Configure a CentOS 8.1 server and do not install `iptables`.
2. `sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/centos/8/tailscale.repo`
3. `sudo dnf install tailscale`
4. `sudo systemctl enable --now tailscaled`
5. At this point, a `sudo systemctl status tailscaled` will show an infinite loop, and `sudo tailscale up` will fail with a missing socket error.

**Expected behavior**
I'd expect that the `iptables-services` package be installed as a dependency of `tailscale` when performing `sudo dnf install tailscale`. I manually did this after seeing this error, and everything worked great.

**Error Message**
Note that `rvpc-gateway` is the hostname of my VPS.

response.title: Switch logtail to send concatenated JSON
response.body:
logtail currently submits batches of log entries as a single JSON array. This makes it a bit annoying to decode on the server side, because we have to do a bit of a dance to do a streaming decode.

We should make logtail instead use "concatenated JSON", i.e. a sequence of standalone JSON blobs with no separators. This is trivial to decode incrementally with the stdlib JSON decoder.

response.title: Support tailscaled in networks requiring HTTP(s)/SOCKs proxies
response.body:
Currently tailscaled (probably) doesn't support networks that require HTTP(s) or SOCKS proxies to access the Internet.

But all the Go packages we use can pretty much handle that already, so it shouldn't be much effort of us to support it. (at least for a DERP-only mode) We don't dial out in too many places.

response.title: Faster restarts: distribute a "node epoch" via control
response.body:
As we're preparing to turn off eager handshaking, restarting tailscaled suddenly has a larger effect on connectivity. Witness hello.ipn.dev:
  - I'm pinging it, everything's fine. My tailscaled handshaked on first packet out, we have session keys, everything's lovely.
  - I restart tailscaled on hello.ipn.dev. Naturally, it forgets all its negotiated session keys. It comes back up, syncs with control, and sits there, waiting for people to handshake with it.
  - Meanwhile, my laptop's still sending pings using the old session key (they get dropped at the receiving end, naturally), and wondering why nothing's coming back. WireGuard by design has no way for us to say "yo I don't know who you are or what you're doing, handshake me"
  - Eventually, my laptop's tailscaled hits the key rotation timer, re-handshakes, and pings start flowing again.

IOW, every tailscaled restart is now potentially up to 2 minutes of downtime before we re-establish.

A common distributed systems way of solving this is epochs: each client reports some epoch number. We could just use a random int64 generated on startup. If you receive a netmap and a peer's epoch has changed, you immediately know that its session keys have been trashed, and you should immediately expire your timers and re-handshake (with some jitter to desynchronize clients from control's simultaneous notification).

Alternatively, we have to guarantee that control will always deliver a sequence of netmaps in which the peer is entirely removed, then added back, and rely on our reconfiguration of wgengine to reset timers. But I'd prefer to have some explicit notion that "hey this client may look the same as before, but it's not". Among other things, it gives us the option to implement debouncing in control to reduce update rates, without breaking client semantics.

cc @crawshaw @bradfitz thoughts?

response.title: magicsock: seeing IPv6 roaming from fe80:...%ens18
response.body:
We currently don't add IPv6 interface addresses to our endpoints. (Only the STUN-discovered IPv6 global address.)

But I just saw this in my logs:

```
2020/03/25 08:54:59 magicsock: rx [5v1Zt] from roaming address [fe80::1cc0:3e8b:119e:c2e1%ens18]:53823, set as new priority
```

Two IPv6 VMs on my LAN over their global IPv6 addresses, but a reply came over the `fe80` link-local address, which was unknown to magicsock, so it went into roaming mode.

Perhaps we should add the interface link-local IPv6 addresses to endpoints. (Do we need to do the whole %zone thing too or can we ignore that and not send it to tailcontrol?)

/cc @danderson

┆Issue is synchronized with this [Asana task](https://app.asana.com/0/1171685499906294/1171686740189991) by [Unito](https://www.unito.io/learn-more)

response.title: wgengine/magicsock: a few maps are never deleted from
response.body:
There are a few maps in magicsock.Conn that are never deleted from and presumably grow without bound.

In particular:

```go
addrsByUDP map[udpAddr]*AddrSet // TODO: clean up this map sometime?
```

(the ones keyed by `key.Public` I'm less concerned about)

magicsock doesn't really know the full state of the world, though. It creates wireguard Endpoints and stores them, but don't know when they die, so it doesn't know the full set of them.

I suppose node deletion is rare-ish, but should we wire up some method into magicsock so we know the full set?

Then it'd be easy to trim `addrsByUDP`, once we know the full set of `*AddrSet` `Endpoint`s.

/cc @crawshaw?

response.title: magicsock: don't report derp home to control until derp connected
response.body:
Currently magicsock measures its distance to the DERPs, makes a decision as its DERP home, and then reports it to the control plane concurrently with connecting to that DERP node.

That leaves a small window where control might think a node is on a certain DERP node (and tell peers) but it's not yet.

We should probably delay the netinfo update until after we're actually connected.

Alternatively, stop telling control about DERP homes entirely, and let control get that from the DERP nodes directly. If each DERP node had, say, 10,000 concurrent connections * 32 byte public keys, that's just 320 kB of network transfer from derp->control on control start-up, followed by a long-poll stream if changes. For auth, control can identify itself the same way nodes do: with the naclbox proof. To get control's public key, derp nodes could just ask for it from https://login.tailscale.com/your-pub-key.

/cc @crawshaw @danderson

response.title: Probe for DERP latency over HTTPS if UDP is blocked
response.body:
In a UDP-blocked network, DERP latency checking fails. This is expected, and we have a fallback: use a random DERP server. This guarantees connectivity, but potentially at the cost of higher latency if we pick the wrong one (75% probability currently).

If we get zero response from UDP during netcheck, we should switch to a fallback where we check DERP latency using HTTPS queries to derpX.tailscale.com. This check will take longer (many RTTs), but it should give us good data for UDP-blocked networks.

response.title: `tailscale netcheck` makes it sound like DERP won't work
response.body:
On a UDP-blocked network, `tailscale netcheck` says this:

```
 * Nearest DERP: 0 ()
 * DERP latency:
```

This makes it look like we're saying "DERP doesn't work". In reality what we're saying is "DERP latency checking failed, magicsock will use a random DERP server".

We should be a little more explicit about the meaning of these fields when latency checking fails.

response.title: Load-balanced services
response.body:
Tailscale handles assigning permanent IP addresses to nodes very well. We can then use DNS to assign names, e.g. `john.device, `jane.device`, etc. However, I can't visualise how DNS for _services_ should be handled in an "ideal" Tailscale deployment.

In a transitional deployment, it's straight forward. Services can be registered with a classic load balancer and have a non-Tailscale private IP. DNS points to this IP and Tailscale routes to it using a subnet route with a Linux relay. This is suboptimal as it doesn't fully embrace the Tailscale vision of end-to-end encryption and authorisation.

In an ideal deployment, each instance of the service is registered to the Tailscale network. In a non-autoscaled, long-lived host scenario you could conceivably set up each host on the Tailscale network and add all of them to the DNS response. You'd use Tailscale's ACLs to allow traffic to each one of those hosts.

How would this work with containers that come and go on a regular basis? Or even autoscaling AWS EC2 instances that shouldn't require human intervention? Even if we assume that the app can somehow authenticate itself as a legitimate service X in Tailscale network Y, the ACL language would probably need to change as administrators would want to express "allow connections from user Z to service X".

--

I have no idea what the solution would look like, but I started a thread here as suggested on Hacker News. I hope I've adequately expressed the problem that I'd love to be solved.

commit.message:
derp: add short queues between reader and writer, drop on overload.

This avoids the server blocking on misbehaving or heavily contended
clients. We attempt to drop from the head of the queue to keep
overall queueing time lower.

Also:
 - fixes server->client keepalives, which weren't happening.
 - removes read rate-limiter, deferring instead to kernel-level
   global limiter/fair queuer.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

derp: move write timeout to package constant.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

derp: add per-reason packet drop counter.

In parallel with the summed counter for now, for dashboard migration.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

derp: sprinkle comments and docstrings.

wgengine/magicsock: listen on udp6, use it for STUN, report endpoint

More steps towards IPv6 transport.

We now send it to tailcontrol, which ignores it.

But it doesn't actually actually support IPv6 yet (outside of STUN).

Signed-off-by: Brad Fitzpatrick <bradfitz@tailscale.com>

response.title: tsweb: use ResponseWriter wrapper to log better.
response.body: Also adds tests for StdHandler, because it's getting a bit complex. And a virtual clock type, so as to not have to implement the arrow of time again. StdHandler has to pass through `http.Handler`, `http.Flusher` and `http.Hijacker` in order to support all our HTTP servers. This leads to a small menagerie of wrappers, in order to correctly handle cases where the underlying ResponseWriter doesn't implement some of the optionals (which can happen in our servers). I believe the wrapper logic works correctly regardless of which underlying interfaces are provided vs. used. Please check carefully. --- This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/tailscale/tailscale/194)

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+package testy
+
+import "time"
+
+// Clock is a testing clock that advances every time its Now method is
+// called, beginning at Start.
+//
+// The zero value starts virtual time at an arbitrary value recorded
+// in Start on the first call to Now, and increments by one second
+// between calls to Now.
+type Clock struct {
+	// Start is the first value returned by Now.
+	Start time.Time
+	// Step is how much to advance with each Now call.
+	// Zero means 1 second.
+	Step time.Duration
+	// Present is the time that the next Now call will receive.
+	Present time.Time
+}
+
+// Now returns the virtual clock's current time, and avances it
+// according to its step configuration.
+func (c *Clock) Now() time.Time {
+	if c.Start.IsZero() {
+		c.Start = time.Now()
+		c.Present = c.Start
+	}
+	step := c.Step
+	if step == 0 {
+		step = time.Second
+	}
+	ret := c.Present
+	c.Present = c.Present.Add(step)
+	return ret
+}
+
+// Reset rewinds the virtual clock to its start time.
+func (c *Clock) Reset() {
+	c.Present = c.Start
+}

+func (h *noopHijacker) Hijack() (net.Conn, *bufio.ReadWriter, error) {
+	// Hijack "successfully" but don't bother returning a conn.

+	var (
+		handlerCode = func(code int) Handler {
+			return HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) error {
+				w.WriteHeader(code)
+				return nil
+			})
+		}
+		handlerErr = func(code int, err error) Handler {
+			return HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) error {
+				if code != 0 {
+					w.WriteHeader(code)
+				}
+				return err
+			})
+		}
+
+		req = func(ctx context.Context, url string) *http.Request {
+			ret, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil)
+			if err != nil {
+				panic(err)
+			}
+			return ret
+		}
+
+		testErr = errors.New("test error")
+		bgCtx   = context.Background()
+		// canceledCtx, cancel = context.WithCancel(bgCtx)
+		clock = testy.Clock{
+			Start: time.Now(),
+			Step:  time.Second,
+		}
+	)
+	// cancel()
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name     string
+		h        Handler
+		r        *http.Request
+		wantCode int
+		wantLog  AccessLogRecord
+	}{
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns 200",
+			h:        handlerCode(200),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/"),
+			wantCode: 200,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				TLS:        false,
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				Code:       200,
+				RequestURI: "/",
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns 404",
+			h:        handlerCode(404),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 404,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Code:       404,
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns 404 via HTTPError",
+			h:        handlerErr(0, Error(404, "not found", testErr)),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 404,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Err:        testErr.Error(),
+				Code:       404,
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns generic error",
+			h:        handlerErr(0, testErr),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 500,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Err:        testErr.Error(),
+				Code:       500,
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns error after writing response",
+			h:        handlerErr(200, testErr),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 200,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Err:        testErr.Error(),
+				Code:       200,
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler returns HTTPError after writing response",
+			h:        handlerErr(200, Error(404, "not found", testErr)),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 200,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Err:        testErr.Error(),
+				Code:       200,
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name:     "handler does nothing",
+			h:        HandlerFunc(func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) error { return nil }),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 500,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:       clock.Start,
+				Seconds:    1.0,
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Code:       500,
+				Err:        "[unexpected] handler did not respond to the client",
+			},
+		},
+
+		{
+			name: "handler hijacks conn",
+			h: HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) error {
+				_, _, err := w.(http.Hijacker).Hijack()
+				if err != nil {
+					t.Errorf("couldn't hijack: %v", err)
+				}
+				return err
+			}),
+			r:        req(bgCtx, "http://example.com/foo"),
+			wantCode: 0,
+			wantLog: AccessLogRecord{
+				When:    clock.Start,
+				Seconds: 1.0,
+
+				Proto:      "HTTP/1.1",
+				Host:       "example.com",
+				Method:     "GET",
+				RequestURI: "/foo",
+				Code:       101,
+			},
+		},
+	}
+
+	for _, test := range tests {
+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			var logs []AccessLogRecord
+			logf := func(fmt string, args ...interface{}) {
+				if fmt == "%s" {
+					logs = append(logs, args[0].(AccessLogRecord))
+				}
+				t.Logf(fmt, args...)
+			}
+
+			clock.Reset()
+
+			rec := noopHijacker{httptest.NewRecorder(), false}
+			// ResponseRecorder defaults Code to 200, grump.
+			rec.Code = 0
+			h := stdHandler(test.h, logf, clock.Now)
+			h.ServeHTTP(&rec, test.r)
+			if rec.Code != test.wantCode {
+				t.Errorf("HTTP code = %v, want %v", rec.Code, test.wantCode)
+			}
+			if !rec.hijacked && !rec.Flushed {
+				t.Errorf("handler didn't flush")
+			}
+			if len(logs) != 1 {
+				t.Errorf("handler didn't write a request log")
+				return
+			}
+			errTransform := cmp.Transformer("err", func(e error) string {
+				if e == nil {
+					return ""
+				}
+				return e.Error()
+			})
+			if diff := cmp.Diff(logs[0], test.wantLog, errTransform); diff != "" {
+				t.Errorf("handler wrote incorrect request log (-got+want):\n%s", diff)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}

commit.message:
testy: add a virtual clock helper for tests.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

tsweb: use a ResponseWriter wrapper to log more accurately.

Also adds tests, because the logging handler is acquiring a fair
number of branches.

Signed-off-by: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

response.diff_hunk:
@@ -155,64 +157,158 @@ type Handler interface {
 	ServeHTTPErr(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) error
 }
 
+// HandlerFunc is an adapter to allow the use of ordinary functions as
+// Handlers. If f is a function with the appropriate signature,
+// HandlerFunc(f) is a Handler that calls f.
+type HandlerFunc func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) error
+
+func (h HandlerFunc) ServeHTTPErr(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) error {
+	return h(w, r)
+}
+
+// StdHandler converts a Handler into a standard http.Handler.
+// Handled requests and any errors returned by h are logged using
+// logf. Errors are handled as specified by the Handler interface.

+

+package tsweb
+
+import (
+	"encoding/json"
+	"fmt"
+	"strings"
+	"time"
+)
+
+// Msg is a structured event log entry.
+type Msg struct {
+	Where    string        `json:"where"`
+	When     time.Time     `json:"when"`
+	Duration time.Duration `json:"duration,omitempty"`
+	Domain   string        `json:"domain,omitempty"`
+	Msg      string        `json:"msg,omitempty"`
+	Err      error         `json:"err,omitempty"`
+	HTTP     *MsgHTTP      `json:"http,omitempty"`
+	Data     interface{}   `json:"data,omitempty"`
+}
+
+// MsgHTTP contains information about the processing of one HTTP
+// request.
+type MsgHTTP struct {
+	Code       int    `json:"code"`
+	Path       string `json:"path"`
+	RemoteAddr string `json:"remote_addr"`
+	UserAgent  string `json:"user_agent"`
+	Referer    string `json:"referer"`
+}
+
+// String returns m as a JSON string.
+func (m Msg) String() string {
+	if m.When.IsZero() {
+		m.When = time.Now()
+	}
+	var buf strings.Builder
+	json.NewEncoder(&buf).Encode(m)
+	ret := buf.String()
+	return ret[:len(ret)-1] // remove trailing newline
+}
+
+// HTTPError is an error with embedded HTTP response information.
+type HTTPError struct {
+	Code int
+	Msg  string // sent to the end-user
+	Err  error
+}
+
+// Error implements the error interface.
+func (e HTTPError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("httperror{%d, %q, %v}", e.Code, e.Msg, e.Err) }
+
+// Error returns an HTTPError containing the given information.
+func Error(code int, msg string, err error) HTTPError {
+	return HTTPError{Code: code, Msg: msg, Err: err}
+}

commit.message:
wgengine/magicsock: don't interrupt endpoint updates, merge all mutex into one

Before, endpoint updates were constantly being interrupted and resumed
on Linux due to tons of LinkChange messages from over-zealous Linux
netlink messages (from router_linux.go)

Now that endpoint updates are fast and bounded in time anyway, just
let them run to completion, but note that another needs to be
scheduled after.

Now logs went from pages of noise to just:

root@taildoc:~# grep -i -E 'stun|endpoint update' log

2020/03/13 08:51:30 magicsock.Conn.ReSTUN: endpoint update active, need another later ("link-change-minor")
2020/03/13 08:51:31 magicsock.Conn: starting endpoint update (link-change-minor)
2020/03/13 08:51:31 magicsock.Conn.ReSTUN: endpoint update active, need another later ("link-change-minor")
2020/03/13 08:51:33 magicsock.Conn: starting endpoint update (link-change-minor)
2020/03/13 08:51:33 magicsock.Conn.ReSTUN: endpoint update active, need another later ("link-change-minor")
2020/03/13 08:51:35 magicsock.Conn: starting endpoint update (link-change-minor)
2020/03/13 08:51:35 magicsock.Conn.ReSTUN: endpoint update active, need another later ("link-change-minor")

2020/03/13 08:46:09 magicsock.Conn: starting endpoint update (periodic)
2020/03/13 08:46:21 magicsock.Conn: starting endpoint update (link-change-major)

response.title: FR: Connect to multiple tailnets simultaneously
response.body:
(edited by Tailscalar to add context on 2022/09/14)
### What are you trying to do?
Log into multiple tailscale accounts at once, on the same device, to access all the machines on both networks simultaneously.

**FR to switch between accounts quickly, and _only_ be able to access machines on one tailnet at a time: https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/713**

--- Original content ---

We use Tailscale at work, and I'd like to use Tailscale at home. As such I want to be able to connect to the two networks simultaneously. When I was using `relay-node`, I created two separate systemd services with separate `--tun`s and `--port`s. When I switched to `tailscaled`, I had to work through all of that again, updating my service files to look like the default one.

It seems like my solution is probably not the best one. Is there a way that a single `tailscaled` process could manage the two networks?

+	s := NewServer(serverPrivateKey, t.Logf)
+	defer s.Close()
+	s.WriteTimeout = 100 * time.Millisecond
+
+	// We send two streams of messages:
+	//
+	//	alice --> bob
+	//	alice --> cathy
+	//
+	// Then cathy stops processing messsages.
+	// That should not interfere with alice talking to bob.
+
+	newClient := func(name string, k key.Private) (c *Client, clientConn nettest.Conn) {
+		t.Helper()
+		c1, c2 := nettest.NewConn(name, 1024)
+		go s.Accept(c1, bufio.NewReadWriter(bufio.NewReader(c1), bufio.NewWriter(c1)), name)
+
+		brw := bufio.NewReadWriter(bufio.NewReader(c2), bufio.NewWriter(c2))

+
+	errCh := make(chan error, 4)
+	recvAndCount := func(count *expvar.Int, name string, client *Client) {

+			b := make([]byte, 1<<9)
+			m, err := client.Recv(b)
+			if err != nil {
+				errCh <- fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", name, err)
+				return
+			}
+			switch m := m.(type) {
+			default:
+				errCh <- fmt.Errorf("%s: unexpected message type %T", name, m)
+				return
+			case ReceivedPacket:
+				if m.Source.IsZero() {
+					errCh <- fmt.Errorf("%s: zero Source address in ReceivedPacket", name)
+					return
+				}
+				count.Add(1)
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	go recvAndCount(&aliceCount, "alice", aliceClient)
+	go recvAndCount(&bobCount, "bob", bobClient)
+	go recvAndCount(&cathyCount, "cathy", cathyClient)
+
+	var cancel func()
+	go func() {
+		t := time.NewTicker(2 * time.Millisecond)
+		defer t.Stop()
+		var ctx context.Context
+		ctx, cancel = context.WithCancel(context.Background())
+		for {
+			select {
+			case <-t.C:
+			case <-ctx.Done():
+				errCh <- nil
+				return
+			}
+
+			msg1 := []byte("hello alice->bob\n")
+			if err := aliceClient.Send(bobKey.Public(), msg1); err != nil {
+				errCh <- fmt.Errorf("alice send to bob: %w", err)
+				return
+			}
+			msg2 := []byte("hello alice->cathy\n")
+
+			// TODO: an error is expected here.
+			// We ignore it, maybe we should log it somehow?
+			aliceClient.Send(cathyKey.Public(), msg2)
+		}
+	}()
+
+	var countSnapshot [3]int64
+	loadCounts := func() (adiff, bdiff, cdiff int64) {
+		t.Helper()
+
+		atotal := aliceCount.Value()
+		btotal := bobCount.Value()
+		ctotal := cathyCount.Value()
+
+		adiff = atotal - countSnapshot[0]
+		bdiff = btotal - countSnapshot[1]
+		cdiff = ctotal - countSnapshot[2]
+
+		countSnapshot[0] = atotal
+		countSnapshot[1] = btotal
+		countSnapshot[2] = ctotal
+
+		t.Logf("count diffs: alice=%d, bob=%d, cathy=%d", adiff, bdiff, cdiff)
+		return adiff, bdiff, cdiff
+	}
+
+	t.Run("initial send", func(t *testing.T) {
+		time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond)
+		a, b, c := loadCounts()
+		if a != 0 {
+			t.Errorf("alice diff=%d, want 0", a)
+		}
+		if b == 0 {
+			t.Errorf("no bob diff, want positive value")
+		}
+		if c == 0 {
+			t.Errorf("no cathy diff, want positive value")
+		}
+	})
+
+	t.Run("block cathy", func(t *testing.T) {
+		// Block cathy. Now the cathyConn buffer will fill up quickly,
+		// and the derp server will back up.
+		cathyConn.SetReadBlock(true)
+		time.Sleep(2 * s.WriteTimeout)
+
+		a, b, _ := loadCounts()
+		if a != 0 {
+			t.Errorf("alice diff=%d, want 0", a)
+		}
+		if b == 0 {

+		}

+		}
+	})

+	cathyConn.Close()

net/nettest: new package with net-like testing primitives

This is a lot like wiring up a local UDP socket, read and write
deadlines work. The big difference is the Block feature, which
lets you stop the packet flow without breaking the connection.
This lets you emulate broken sockets and test timeouts actually
work.

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

derp: introduce Conn interface

This lets us test with something other than a net.Conn.

derp: do not treat failure to relay as the fault of the sender

If Alice attempts to send a packet to Bob and the DERP server
encounters an error on the socket to Bob, we should not disconnect
Alice for that.

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

derp: use a write timeout when sending to clients

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

derp: test that client a->b and a->c relaying do not interfere

Without the recent write deadline introduction, this test fails.

They still do interfere, but the interference is now bound by
the write deadline. Many improvements are possible.

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

response.body:
We'd like to be able to distribute automated, unsigned DMG images of the latest macOS client.

But unsigned means no NetworkExtension, which means we need to use cmd/tailscaled as the backend, with its utun device. WireGuard TUN supports that, but we don't have implementations of wgengine/router to do that.

Ignoring the GUI glue, I can log in to tailscaled on a Mac:

```
$ sudo mkdir -p /Library/tailscaled
$ sudo tailscaled --state=/Library/tailscaled/tailscaled.state --tun=utun4
```

... and then `tailscale up` as a regular user to get my login URL & add the machine.

And then I see it form the mesh and do the handshakes, but I don't have routes.

response.title: magicsock: NotePreferred call only partially works
response.body:
On trying to send a packet to a DERP server, we call `derphttp.NewClient`. It is then immediately followed by a NotePreferred call, which sets the preferred field in the derphttp client. But as the
connection is established lazily, c.client  == nil. That means the bit is not sent to the server until `connect` is called. But that only sends the bit if preferred==true.

Moreover, later when `NotePreferred` is called again, the preferred field in the derphttp client has already been set, so then the bit is never sent to the DERP server.

The result is we do not send preferred==false to DERP servers.

response.title: stunner: re-do how Stunner works
response.body:
It used to make assumptions based on having Anycast IPs that are super
near. Now we're intentionally going to a bunch of different distant
IPs to measure latency.

Also, optimize how the hairpin detection works. No need to STUN on
that socket. Just use that separate socket for sending, once we know
the other UDP4 socket's endpoint. The trick is: make our test probe
also a STUN packet, so it fits through magicsock's existing STUN
routing.

This drops netcheck from ~5 seconds to ~250-500ms.

Signed-off-by: Brad Fitzpatrick <bradfitz@tailscale.com>

commit.message:
stunner: re-do how Stunner works

It used to make assumptions based on having Anycast IPs that are super
near. Now we're intentionally going to a bunch of different distant
IPs to measure latency.

Also, optimize how the hairpin detection works. No need to STUN on
that socket. Just use that separate socket for sending, once we know
the other UDP4 socket's endpoint. The trick is: make our test probe
also a STUN packet, so it fits through magicsock's existing STUN
routing.

This drops netcheck from ~5 seconds to ~250-500ms.

Signed-off-by: Brad Fitzpatrick <bradfitz@tailscale.com>

response.body: Doesn't this also need the lock?
At least half the DERP servers will take 100-200ms to respond, so this will always retry at least once. Still a bit aggressive?
only 2?

It's owned by Run in its main goroutine, which sets it on entry and clears it on exit.

Nothing else can call it concurrently once inFlight has been zeroed. I'll add a comment.

I'm always reluctant to "over lock" things because it get confusing to readers in the future. I'd rather have it be as tight as possible and catch mistakes early if invariants get violated.
Actually I'm just going to delete the onPacket clear. It was mostly for debugging. It's not required for correctness. The GC will deal with it.

I ended this change a bit early because it was getting big and I got to a good stopping point. The further plan is to collect a couple STUN pings from each node (to help with #162), as long as we can within an overall limit (like 750ms or 1ms or the time to collect a minimum 1 STUN ping from each node).

And then we'll limit the number of STUN pings for the DERPs likely to still be far away. So we'll only be more paranoid-ly timing our close ones (say, NY and SF if you're in the US). But we do want multiple in the general case. It's just that I'm currently throwing those away. Later I'll both keep those, and have netcheck keep a few history netcheck.Report records.

This is to limit damage for now until the next step where it more intelligently collects multiple STUN pings (as replied to Dave above)

Plus I think even 1 would be fine for our use cases.

response.title: Create a Nix derivation and Nixos module for tailscaled
response.body:
https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/78008 was my initial attempt, using the old pre-OSS relaynode binaries. Now that we have an OSS linux client, it makes sense to build the derivation directly from this repo.

One thing we need to watch out for when making those packages: when building from just the OSS repo, currently we don't build a very good version stamp into the binaries. This is important for us because we use that version stamp to track the state of the Tailscale fleet (what versions are active), so it'd suck to start distributing `vTODO` binaries :). Options for this:
  - In the derivation build, overwrite version/version.go with a generated file that uses `git describe --always` to embed the OSS commit ID.
  - Use the version stamp that's currently in there. It's a date-based stamp that's occasionally updated by @bradfitz. It's easy (no magic needed in nix derivation), but the version stamp is less precise than the option above.
  - Don't build from source, instead grab the static binary tarballs from https://pkgs.tailscale.com/ and just repackage those binaires. They have no external dependencies, so it would be easy, and those binaries contain the version info generated from our corp (non-OSS) repo. But, those binaries aren't 100% reproducible from source, so, :/.

cc @martinbaillie, who expressed interest in nix/nixos packaging.

response.title: Home DERP server glitches
response.body:
Plotted a new DERP graph, of home connections over time by DERP location. It reveals that 1 node appears to be glitching occasionally between SF and NYC:

![derp](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1918/76153716-a0538880-6084-11ea-8950-d20e16d03325.png)

The glitch doesn't last very long, but there's fairly clearly a decrease by 1 in SF, matched by an increase of 1 in NYC, and then the reverse a short time later.

This is likely contributing to additional netmap updates, and probably DERP packetloss stats during the window where the home connection has migrated but other nodes haven't updated yet.

Hypotheses for cause:
 1. SFO sometimes fails to respond, causing node to flip to next best DERP?
 2. Node is roughly equidistant to SFO and NYC, occasional latency fluctuations cause a flip?
 3. Incorrect home DERP selection logic? (feels unlikely, or we'd see a lot more glitching)

If 1 or 2 is true, tracking a window of probes and having some hysteresis for switching home DERPs may be indicated.

response.title: Test flake: Bursts of lost packets wgengine/magicsock.TestTwoDevicePing
response.body:
As we grind down the issues revealed by the new magicsock test, a new failure mode has bubbled to the top: the test reports bursts of 10-20 packets missing during ping tests.

The root cause (confirmed by DERP_DEBUG_LOGS=1 on the failing test run) is a race in the establishment of DERP connections in the test harness: we have no way to wait for the two test devices to handshake with their home DERP server before we begin DERP testing. If we start transmitting pings before the home connections are established, the DERP server (correctly) drops the relayed packets, since it has no viable forwarding target.

The code itself is working as intended, there is a small startup time during which we may be unable to route packets. It does not affect normal operation of Tailscale, but the tests obviously trigger this reliably.

For testing purposes, we either need a helper that can block on a magicsock Conn until home DERP connections are up, or we must relax the test to allow for initial packetloss until there is reliable transmission, and then switch to its current strict "no loss" behavior.

@bradfitz thoughts on which is preferable? Altering the test feels better to me, as it'll be accurately testing the real-world behavior of magicsock, rather than add a synchronization crutch that only tests use... OTOH I see the value in being able to eliminate known, by-design startup races from tests so that our synthetic cases can more precisely test specific behaviors.

response.title: DERP magicsock integration sometimes drops packets
response.body:
The current implementation of ReceiveIPv4 in magicsock is racey, because it's reading packets from two sources: a UDP conn for p2p traffic, and DERP machinery for relayed packets. It's possible for both sources to yield a packet simultaneously, but we can only return one from ReceiveIPv4.

One leg of the receive `select` deliberately throws away the non-DERP packet and delivers the DERP one. This causes "mysterious" packet losses in tests that involve DERP, even on localhost<>localhost traffic.

We should be able to solve this with a 1-packet buffer in magicsock, which stores the race's "loser" and yields it on the next ReceiveIPv4 call ahead of attempting another network read.

response.title: derp: DERP Return Path Optimization (DRPO)
response.body:
Currently DERP does asymmetric routing. If A and B have different home nodes (say, SF and NY), then A sends to B via NY and B sends to A via SF.

But there's an optimization we could do:

One of the packets has to arrive first. When A (connected to its home node SF), gets a packet from B via DERP SF, it can add a "DERP routing table entry" for that public key to go via that specific DERP TCP connection, keeping that routing entry alive until either: a) the TCP connection dies (for whatever reason), or b) the server sends a "previous sender disconnected" frame.

So then the server would just need to keep track of all the public keys that have sent a node a message, and upon a TCP connection, the DERP SF server can tell A that B is disconnected, and A can remove its routing table entry.

So now, when A wants to send a reply packet (or any packet) to B, it first looks to see if it has an explicit DERP route for B, otherwise it falls back to using B's DERP home node. That also means less latency on the first reply, since it doesn't need to do the TCP+TLS+DERP round trips to set up the connection. And it minimizes overall connections & memory use.

Again, this is just an optimization (that should trigger a lot; we could add varz) and the fallback behavior would be the same as today.

/cc @crawshaw @danderson

wgengine/magicsock: only set addrByKey once in CreateEndpoint.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

wgengine/magicsock: fix destination selection logic to work with DERP.

The effect is subtle: when we're not spraying packets, and have not yet
figured out a curAddr, and we're not spraying, we end up sending to
whatever the first IP is in the iteration order. In English, that
means "when we have no idea where to send packets, and we've given
up on sending to everyone, just send to the first addr we see in
the list."

This is, in general, what we want, because the addrs are in sorted
preference order, low to high, and DERP is the least preferred
destination. So, when we have no idea where to send, send to DERP,
right?

... Except for very historical reasons, appendDests iterated through
addresses in _reverse_ order, most preferred to least preferred.
crawshaw@ believes this was part of the earliest handshaking
algorithm magicsock had, where it slowly iterated through possible
destinations and poked handshakes to them one at a time.

Anyway, because of this historical reverse iteration, in the case
described above of "we have no idea where to send", the code would
end up sending to the _most_ preferred candidate address, rather
than the _least_ preferred. So when in doubt, we'd end up firing
packets into the blackhole of some LAN address that doesn't work,
and connectivity would not work.

This case only comes up if all your non-DERP connectivity options
have failed, so we more or less failed to detect it because we
didn't have a pathological test box deployed. Worse, codependent
bug 2839854994f204a9e95e4d8d410490bb4f25e1fe made DERP accidentally
work sometimes anyway by incorrectly exploiting roamAddr behavior,
albeit at the cost of making DERP traffic symmetric. In fixing
DERP to once again be asymmetric, we effectively removed the
bandaid that was concealing this bug.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

wgengine/magicsock: check all 3 fast paths independently.

The previous code would skip the DERP short-circuit if roamAddr
was set, which is not what we wanted. More generally, hitting
any of the fast path conditions is a direct return, so we can
just have 3 standalone branches rather than 'else if' stuff.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

wgengine/magicsock: fix packet spraying test to (mostly) pass.

It previously passed incorrectly due to bugs. With those fixed,
it becomes flaky for 2 reasons. One of them is the wireguard handshake
race, which can eat the 1st sprayed packet and prevent roamAddr
discovery. This change fixes that failure, by spreading the test
traffic out enough that additional spraying occurs.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

commit.message:
wgengine/magicsock: never set a DERP server as a roamAddr.

DERP traffic is asymmetric by design, with nodes always sending
to their peer's home DERP server. However, if roamAddr is set,
magicsock will always push data there, rather than let DERP
server selection do its thing, so we end up accidentally
creating a symmetric flow.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <danderson@tailscale.com>

response.body:
Add some commentary to the commit message please:

As DERP connections are asymmetric, with each node sending to its home DERP node, recording the sender's DERP home results in unexpectedly symmetric conversations via DERP.

response.title: Routing loops/sticky sockets: don't route tailscaled traffic through tailscale routes
response.body:
Classic VPN problem: VPN installs routes, the VPN's daemon's own traffic starts going over the VPN, and everything craps out.

There's various hacks to make this work, which are well documented at https://www.wireguard.com/netns/ . We need to do something like this in tailscaled on linux.

Weirdly, there is one method that's not listed on the Wireguard page, and which I think is basically perfect for our needs: policy routing's `suppress_ifgroup` option. `man ip-rule` says:

```
              suppress_ifgroup GROUP
                     reject routing decisions that use a device belonging to
                     the interface group GROUP.
```

Translated a bit: if we make an interface group `tailscale`, and add `tailscale0` to that group, we have a way to express "route these packets as if tailscale0 didn't exist", which is exactly what we want.

All that remains from there, is to mark packets that originate from `tailscaled`, and push them through a slightly different set of routing policies. Aside from that, we can continue business as usual and have everything work out. Sketch of proof below.

Before tailscaled, the network stack looks something like this:

```
# ip rule
0:	from all lookup local
32766:	from all lookup main
32767:	from all lookup default

# ip route show table main
default via 192.168.16.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 600
192.168.16.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.16.10 metric 600 
```

Tailscaled comes up, connects to control, receives a configuration that pushes `0.0.0.0/0` to some other node. It does the following to configure networking:
 1. Create interface `tailscale0`, via tuntap.
 2. Run `ip link set dev tailscale0 group 5189`, which places the interface in the `5189` interface group (careful: `ip link add` also has a `group` option, but that one mucks with multicast groups)
 3. Run `ip rule add priority 5189 fwmark 5189 table main suppress_ifgroup 5189`
 4. Run `ip rule add priority 5190 fwmark 5189 table 5189`
 5. Run `ip route add unreachable 0.0.0.0/0 table 5189`
 6. Bring up `tailscale0`, add preferred default route: `ip route add default via 100.101.102.103 dev tailscale0 metric 10`
 7. tailscaled sets SO_MARK=5189 on all sockets it makes, both listeners and dial-outs.

Network stack now looks like this:

```
# ip rule
0:	from all lookup local
5189:	from all fwmark 0x1445 lookup main suppress_ifgroup 5189
5190:	from all fwmark 0x1445 lookup 5189
32766:	from all lookup main
32767:	from all lookup default

# ip route show table main
default via 100.101.102.103 dev tailscale0 proto kernel metric 10
default via 192.168.16.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 600
192.168.16.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.16.10 metric 600 

# ip route show table 5189
unreachable default
```

Packet flow for a random ping packet:
 - Rules 5189 and 5190 don't match (wrong fwmark). Execute route lookup in table main.
 - Match `default via 100.101.102.103 dev tailscale0`, push packet into tailscale0.
 - tailscaled receives packet, does fun stuff to it, eventually transmits a wireguard packet out its UDP socket.
 - Rule 5189 matches because UDP socket set fwmark 5189. Execute route lookup in table main, suppressing ifgroup tailscale.
 - Match `default via 192.168.16.1 dev eth0`, push packet out eth0.

Misc points:
 - Rule 5190 is there to prevent a fallthrough into a general routing table lookup, which would create a routing loop. If the suppressed lookup fails, we want that to be a hard "address unreachable".
 - 5189 is the keys above "tail". We will probably have to exercise more care in selecting the fwmark, since some sysadmins use it as a bitmask.
 - Partially cleans up after itself on crash. Routes via tailscale0 are removed, which is enough for the network stack to revert to VPN-less behavior. IP rules and the 5189 routing table linger harmlessly. Obviously we clean those up on normal exit.

Concerns:
 - We have to SO_MARK every socket in tailscaled. Unmarked sockets will use VPN routes. We could make the IP rules match on a UID range, if we get tailscaled running as its own user with capabilities granting privileges. However this would break just running tailscaled as root without a service daemon to set things up right.
 - Maybe this doesn't actually work as documented? I'm worried that it doesn't appear in the WireGuard rundown of options, even though it's very close to the SO_NOTOIF patch Jason tried to upstream.

┆Issue is synchronized with this [Asana task](https://app.asana.com/0/1171685499906294/1171687219118753) by [Unito](https://www.unito.io/learn-more)

response.title: Implement `tailscale powerwash`
response.body:
Talking to some folks who bake VM images for deployment, they would like a way to install Tailscale, maybe connect to a network during the baking process to pull some data, but then remove all Tailscale state from the machine, so that when the baked image is cloned 100 times we don't end up with 100 copies of the same machine key lying around.

`tailscaled` should do that as much as possible by default (i.e. don't create machine keys until the first operator interaction via something like `tailscale up`), but for cases where you've actively used tailscale but then want to revert it to factory settings, we should have a command for that.

Roughly, two possible implementations:
 - systemctl stop tailscaled && rm -rf stuff && systemctl start tailscaled
 - implement the powerwash in tailscaled itself, via an RPC command. Gets a bit trickier in multi-user environments, because did you want to wipe just your user's state? All state? Are you allowed to wipe all state?

This will only start to _really_ matter once we have automated enrollment options, because until then it's less useful to bake Tailscale into VM images.

response.title: paths: use /var/db for state on BSDs, and /var/run for sockets.
response.body:
On BSD, /var/db is what linux calls /var/lib.

On modern linux, /run and /var/run are the same directory, but
on BSD the correct path is /var/run, so use that.

Fixes #79

response.title: derp: switch from expvar to prometheus metrics.
response.body:
This is what it takes to monitor derp with prometheus/grafana. Efficiency is about same or better, prometheus does integer-ey things with atomic ops.

Could also use the OpenTelemetry libraries which do much the same, but also offer distributed tracing if we ever wanted it. They're still alpha though so I skipped.

response.body:
This PR is working the linker's DCE optimization pretty heavily to keep a mountain of code out of  tailscaled. Does it work? What's the effect on binary size?

Philosophically, I'm pretty sad about this. At its core, this huge Prometheus package must have a handful of atomics per number at most, but now every leaf package needs dependencies on things like the proto library? If all those dependencies came in package main to actually send the numbers over the wire that wouldn't really bother me too much, but dragging them around everywhere feels like programming in google3. Is there no lightweight metrics library out there?

Alternatively, could we use this thingy so we only need to import the client_golang in derper's main? https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/master/prometheus/expvar_collector.go

Philosophically, I'd like the shortest path to some monitoring, and this is that :). I agree that the client is larger than it should have to be, but I'd also point out that binary size isn't relevant to the servers we want to instrument. I'm still not happy adding large closures, obviously, but on balance I'd still rather have monitoring.

re: expvar collector, the docs note: `Note that the data models of expvar and Prometheus are fundamentally different, and that the expvar Collector is inherently slower than native Prometheus metrics. Thus, the expvar Collector is probably great for experiments and prototying, but you should seriously consider a more direct implementation of Prometheus metrics for monitoring production systems.`

I don't much care about the performance aspect, but the data model mismatch is going to cause us pain when things like counter don't quite behave right.

I don't know of any lighter weight metric libraries that are compatible with the modern monitoring ecosystem. One possibility might be opentelemetry, which aggressively splits stuff into sub-packages, but I don't know if that actually reduces the cross-dependencies between them.
This branch adds 1.6MiB to cmd/derper, so your fears about code bloat are definitely justified though.

The expvar HTTP handler is a few lines:

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/c4ca60313ef7fd0b9d2c223889caeb20147309ac/src/expvar/expvar.go#L332

Can't we just write our own HTTP handler in the format that Prometheus wants?

(Format: https://github.com/prometheus/docs/blob/master/content/docs/instrumenting/exposition_formats.md)

My concern is that I'd like to add a bunch of varz to tailscaled too and that ends up in the NetworkExtension and I'd prefer if we could use the same counter types everywhere. expvar seems light.

`Note that the data models of expvar and Prometheus are fundamentally different`

If you want to lick that cookie and debug the monitoring when it fails, I'm okay sticking with expvar.

Of note is that we lose all the more advanced metric types, e.g. histograms. We'll also need some wrapper around expvar to define whether variables are counters or gauges (which influences the semantics of how decrements and resets are handled, to correctly preserve rate data).

> We'll also need some wrapper around expvar to define whether variables are counters or gauges

We can have naming conventions, then our HTTP handler understands those conventions and maps it to the right prometheus type.

Implying variable names that contain their type information, even though the prometheus format separates the two :(.

Lemme give the opentelemetry library a try before we go this route. They seem to have designed stuff to avoid bloat and make the specific implementation selectable in main(). I'd feel more comfortable with a grown-up telemetry library as a base.

Never mind, the API is awful. Somehow more verbose than prometheus's.

Okay, let's do expvar munging then :((

FYI: my biggest concern above was the new dependency that's in the derp package, which is imported in tailscaled and iOS. So we are relying on the linker pulling it all out for it to not change the iOS binary size.

More generally, it would be great to have a lightweight metrics package everywhere. I'm amazed it doesn't exist already.

Definitely wish something lightweight existed that supports modern
telemetry. Unfortunately the metrics space seems to favor architecture
astronautics, so we're stuck with an impedance mismatch :-(

response.title: When regaining network connectivity, tailscale-relay has to be restarted to get connection to mesh
response.body:
**Describe the bug**
When changing networks or losing and regaining network connectivity, i.e., moving from home to work, changing access points, etc.., tailscale-relay loses connectivity to all mesh nodes until the service is restarted (with systemctl restart tailscale-relay for instance)

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Connect to mesh network on a laptop
3. Test mesh network, i.e., via ping hello.ipn.dev
2. Lose and regain network connectivity
3. Test mesh network again, i.e., via ping hello.ipn.dev
4. No connectivity

**Expected behavior**
Connectivity should be regained automatically

**Version information:**
 - Device: Dell Inspiron XPS 7590
 - OS: Fedora Workstation 31
 - OS version: Fedora Workstation 31, Linux kernel 5.5.6-201.fc31.x86_64
 - Tailscale version: tailscale-relay-0.94-236.x86_64

**Additional context**
This happens very reliably.

response.title: magicsock: DERP and roaming address oscillation
response.body:
morty's logs see a lot of:

```
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641, set as new priority
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from known 127.3.3.40:1 (0), replaces roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641, set as new priority
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from known 127.3.3.40:1 (0), replaces roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641, set as new priority
magicsock: rx [pub:…e4Vj] from known 127.3.3.40:1 (0), replaces roaming address 207.108.197.248:41641
```

According to CONTROL this is one of @danderson 's machines, which has somehow roamed onto a new port (CONTROL thinks it is on 207.108.197.248:1394). That's pretty interesting, I guess this is an example of us needing to STUN more.

But in magicsock is means we have a lot of log noise talking to it. Spray packets come in from both DERP and the roaming address, meaning in `AddrSet` we swap address priority a lot.

Should we make less log noise? Avoid replacing roaming addresses?

cc @danderson @bradfitz

will change a bunch in the future, but this is good enough to launch on parity
with relaynode.

commit.message:
cmd/tailscale: switch to an ffcli based CLI.

Two commands for now, `up` and `netcheck`. The commands and the flags they take
will change a bunch in the future, but this is good enough to launch on parity
with relaynode.

Signed-Off-By: David Anderson <dave@natulte.net>

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+// Package opt defines optional types.
+package opt
+
+import (
+	"fmt"
+	"strconv"
+)
+
+// Bool represents an optional boolean to be JSON-encoded.
+// The string can be empty (for unknown or unspecified), or
+// "true" or "false".
+type Bool string
+
+func (b *Bool) Set(v bool) {
+	*b = Bool(strconv.FormatBool(v))
+}
+
+func (b *Bool) Clear() { *b = "" }
+
+func (b Bool) Get() (v bool, ok bool) {
+	if b == "" {
+		return
+	}
+	v, err := strconv.ParseBool(string(b))
+	return v, err == nil
+}
+
+var (
+	trueBytes  = []byte("true")
+	falseBytes = []byte("false")
+	nullBytes  = []byte("null")
+)
+
+func (b Bool) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
+	switch b {
+	case "true":
+		return trueBytes, nil
+	case "false":
+		return falseBytes, nil
+	case "":
+		return nullBytes, nil
+	}
+	return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid opt.Bool value %q", string(b))
+}
+
+func (b *Bool) UnmarshalJSON(j []byte) error {
+	// Note: written with a bunch of ifs instead of a switch
+	// because I'm sure the Go compiler optimizes away these
+	// []byte->string allocations in an == comparison, but I'm too
+	// lazy to check whether that's true in a switch also.
+	if string(j) == "true" {
+		*b = "true"
+		return nil
+	}
+	if string(j) == "false" {
+		*b = "false"
+		return nil
+	}
+	if string(j) == "null" {
+		*b = ""
+		return nil
+	}
+	return fmt.Errorf("invalid opt.Bool value %q", j)
+}

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+// Package netcheck checks the network conditions from the current host.
+package netcheck
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"io"
+	"net"
+	"strings"
+	"sync"
+	"time"
+
+	"golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"
+	"tailscale.com/interfaces"
+	"tailscale.com/stunner"
+	"tailscale.com/types/logger"
+	"tailscale.com/types/opt"
+)
+
+type Report struct {
+	UDP                   bool                     // UDP works
+	IPv6                  bool                     // IPv6 works
+	MappingVariesByDestIP opt.Bool                 // for IPv4
+	DERPLatency           map[string]time.Duration // keyed by STUN host:port
+}
+
+func GetReport(ctx context.Context, logf logger.Logf) (*Report, error) {
+	closeOnCtx := func(c io.Closer) {
+		<-ctx.Done()
+		c.Close()
+	}
+
+	v6, err := interfaces.HaveIPv6GlobalAddress()
+	if err != nil {
+		logf("interfaces: %v", err)
+	}
+	var (
+		mu  sync.Mutex
+		ret = &Report{
+			DERPLatency: map[string]time.Duration{},
+		}
+		gotIP = map[string]string{} // server -> IP
+	)
+	add := func(server, ip string, d time.Duration) {
+		logf("%s says we are %s (in %v)", server, ip, d)
+
+		mu.Lock()
+		defer mu.Unlock()
+		ret.UDP = true
+		ret.DERPLatency[server] = d
+		if strings.Contains(server, "-v6") {
+			ret.IPv6 = true
+		}
+		gotIP[server] = ip
+	}
+
+	var pc4, pc6 net.PacketConn
+
+	pc4, err = net.ListenPacket("udp4", ":0")
+	if err != nil {
+		logf("udp4: %v", err)
+		return nil, err
+	}
+	go closeOnCtx(pc4)
+	if v6 {
+		pc6, err = net.ListenPacket("udp6", ":0")
+		if err != nil {
+			logf("udp6: %v", err)
+			v6 = false
+		} else {
+			go closeOnCtx(pc6)
+		}
+	}
+
+	reader := func(s *stunner.Stunner, pc net.PacketConn) {
+		var buf [64 << 10]byte
+		for {
+			n, addr, err := pc.ReadFrom(buf[:])
+			if err != nil {
+				if ctx.Err() != nil {
+					return
+				}
+				logf("ReadFrom: %v", err)
+				return
+			}
+			ua, ok := addr.(*net.UDPAddr)
+			if !ok {
+				logf("ReadFrom: unexpected addr %T", addr)
+				continue
+			}
+			logf("Packet from %v: %q", ua, buf[:n])
+			s.Receive(buf[:n], ua)
+		}
+
+	}
+
+	var grp errgroup.Group
+	s4 := &stunner.Stunner{
+		Send:     pc4.WriteTo,
+		Endpoint: add,
+		Servers:  []string{"derp1.tailscale.com:3478", "derp2.tailscale.com:3478"},
+		Logf:     logf,
+	}
+	grp.Go(func() error { return s4.Run(ctx) })
+	go reader(s4, pc4)
+
+	if v6 {
+		s6 := &stunner.Stunner{
+			Endpoint: add,
+			Send:     pc6.WriteTo,
+			Servers:  []string{"derp1-v6.tailscale.com:3478", "derp2-v6.tailscale.com:3478"},
+			Logf:     logf,
+			OnlyIPv6: true,
+		}
+		grp.Go(func() error { return s6.Run(ctx) })
+		go reader(s6, pc6)
+	}
+
+	err = grp.Wait()
+	logf("stunner.Run: %v", err)
+
+	mu.Lock()
+	defer mu.Unlock() // unnecessary, but feels weird without
+
+	// TODO: generalize this to find at least two out of N DERP
+	// servers (where N will be 5+).
+	ip1 := gotIP["derp1.tailscale.com:3478"]
+	ip2 := gotIP["derp2.tailscale.com:3478"]
+	if ip1 != "" && ip2 != "" {
+		ret.MappingVariesByDestIP.Set(ip1 != ip2)
+	}
+
+	return ret, nil
+}

response.title: macOS & iOS doesn't use DNS set in the admin panel
response.body:
**Describe the bug**
On macOS dns resolution order doesn't get prioritized with the dns in the admin panel which means it's essentially ignored.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Set the DNS in the admin panel
2. scutil --dns should show the config in the scoped queries
3. ping or resolve a host where the dns would have a different ip ie. using an internal VPC dns in aws to get the internal ip vs the external ip.
4. You'll see the public ip returned not the internal ip. nslookup with the admin dns resolves to the internal ip correctly

**Expected behavior**
I'd expect the dns set in the admin to take priority with the vpn is connected, or at least an option per client to decide

**Version information:**
 - Device: macbook pro
 - OS: macOS
 - OS version: 10.14.6
 - Tailscale version: App version: 0.95.208

**Additional context**
I currently have a very specific hardcoded example that works as a work around at
https://github.com/pelotech/tailscale-tools/tree/master/resolver
it listens to the up/down of the interfaces and adds resolvers for specific domains to be used.

┆Issue is synchronized with this [Asana task](https://app.asana.com/0/1171685499906294/1171687016060361) by [Unito](https://www.unito.io/learn-more)

wgengine: add pinger to generate initial spray packets

For 3 seconds after a successful handshake, wgengine will send a
ping packet every 300ms to its peer. This ensures the spray logic
in magicsock has something to spray.

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

response.title: magicsock: spray some packets after an endpoint change
response.body:
Intended to help with upgrading from DERP to direct UDP connections.

In particular, this is designed to catch the case where a
HandshakeInitiation packet is sent out but the intermediate NATs
have not been primed, so the packet passes over DERP.
In that case, the HandshakeResponse also comes back over DERP,
and the connection proceeds via DERP without ever trying to punch
through the NAT.

With this change, the HandshakeResponse (which was sprayed out
and so primed one NAT) triggers an UpdateDst, which marks the
next 5 non-handshake packets for spraying. At this point both
NATs are primed, one of these 5 packets will make it through,
triggering an UpdateDst on the other side and then both sides
will be talking directly without DERP.

commit.message:
magicsock: spray some normal packets after a handshake

In particular, this is designed to catch the case where a
HandshakeInitiation packet is sent out but the intermediate NATs
have not been primed, so the packet passes over DERP.
In that case, the HandshakeResponse also comes back over DERP,
and the connection proceeds via DERP without ever trying to punch
through the NAT.

With this change, the HandshakeResponse (which was sprayed out
and so primed one NAT) triggers an UpdateDst, which triggers
the extra spray logic.

(For this to work, there has to be an initial supply of packets
to send on to a peer for the three seconds following a handshake.
The source of these packets is left as a future exercise.)

Signed-off-by: David Crawshaw <crawshaw@tailscale.com>

response.title: Magicsock refuses to downgrade from LAN to DERP
response.body:
## Steps to reproduce

Be on bradfitz's LAN.
Block all UDP traffic to/from bradfitz's dev box.
Run tailscaled.
Tailscaled peers with bradfitz's dev box over DERP, because LAN doesn't work.
Remove UDP blocks. Direct LAN connectivity now available.
Tailscaled notices this on the next handshake cycle, upgrades from DERP to LAN \o/
Put UDP blocks back. Direct LAN connectivity is broken.
Notice that tailscaled never downgrades from LAN back to DERP. Connectivity remains broken until you restart tailscaled.

During the outage, tailscaled periodically logs:

Feb 21 15:02:12 vega tailscaled[2996756]: 2020/02/21 15:02:12 magicsock: rx [pub:…xg0R] from low-pri 127.3.3.40:1 (0), keeping current 10.0.128.103:41641 (2)

So it's receiving nothing from LAN, and receiving handshakes from DERP, but refusing to downgrade.

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+// mkpkg builds the Tailscale rpm and deb packages.
+package main
+
+import (
+	"fmt"
+	"log"
+	"os"
+	"strings"
+
+	"github.com/goreleaser/nfpm"
+	_ "github.com/goreleaser/nfpm/deb"
+	_ "github.com/goreleaser/nfpm/rpm"
+	"github.com/pborman/getopt"
+)
+
+// parseFiles parses a comma-separated list of colon-separated pairs
+// into a map of filePathOnDisk -> filePathInPackage.
+func parseFiles(s string) (map[string]string, error) {
+	ret := map[string]string{}
+	for _, f := range strings.Split(s, ",") {
+		fs := strings.Split(f, ":")
+		if len(fs) != 2 {
+			return nil, fmt.Errorf("unparseable file field %q", f)
+		}
+		ret[fs[0]] = fs[1]
+	}
+	return ret, nil
+}
+
+func main() {
+	out := getopt.StringLong("out", 'o', "", "output file to write")
+	goarch := getopt.StringLong("arch", 'a', "amd64", "GOARCH this package is for")
+	pkgType := getopt.StringLong("type", 't', "deb", "type of package to build (deb or rpm)")
+	files := getopt.StringLong("files", 'F', "", "comma-separated list of files in src:dst form")
+	configFiles := getopt.StringLong("configs", 'C', "", "like --files, but for files marked as user-editable config files")
+	version := getopt.StringLong("version", 0, "0.0.0", "version of the package")
+	getopt.Parse()
+
+	filesMap, err := parseFiles(*files)
+	if err != nil {
+		log.Fatalf("Parsing --files: %v", err)
+	}
+	configsMap, err := parseFiles(*configFiles)
+	if err != nil {
+		log.Fatalf("Parsing --configs: %v", err)
+	}
+	info := nfpm.WithDefaults(&nfpm.Info{
+		Name:        "tailscale",
+		Arch:        *goarch,
+		Platform:    "linux",
+		Version:     *version,
+		Maintainer:  "Tailscale Inc <info@tailscale.com>",
+		Description: "The easiest, most secure, cross platform way to use WireGuard + oauth2 + 2FA/SSO",
+		Homepage:    "https://www.tailscale.com",
+		License:     "MIT",
+		Overridables: nfpm.Overridables{
+			Files:       filesMap,
+			ConfigFiles: configsMap,
+		},
+	})
+
+	switch *pkgType {
+	case "deb":
+		info.Section = "net"
+		info.Priority = "extra"
+	case "rpm":
+		info.Overridables.RPM.Group = "Network"
+	}
+
+	pkg, err := nfpm.Get(*pkgType)
+	if err != nil {
+		log.Fatalf("Getting packager for %q: %v", *pkgType, err)
+	}
+
+	f, err := os.Create(*out)
+	if err != nil {
+		log.Fatalf("Creating output file %q: %v", *out, err)
+	}
+	defer f.Close()
+
+	if err := pkg.Package(info, f); err != nil {
+		log.Fatalf("Creating package %q: %v", *out, err)
+	}
+}

response.body:
When we do tailscale binary releases, we stamp version info into the binaries with the Go linker.

But for people just using "go get" the default way, we don't have that info.

Since Go modules, we at least see the summary of all our deps (and Go's version itself; I'm running a devel build) automatically stamped into the binaries:

```
$ go version -m ~/bin/tailscaled
/home/bradfitz/bin/tailscaled: devel +e7f9e17b79 Tue Jan 28 22:08:43 2020 +0000
        path    tailscale.com/cmd/tailscaled

        dep     github.com/pborman/getopt       v0.0.0-20190409184431-ee0cd42419d3      h1:YtFkrqsMEj7YqpIhRteVxJxCeC3jJBieuLr0d4C4rSA=

        dep     golang.org/x/crypto     v0.0.0-20200210222208-86ce3cb69678      h1:wCWoJcFExDgyYx2m2hpHgwz8W3+FPdfldvIgzqDIhyg=
        dep     golang.org/x/net        v0.0.0-20200202094626-16171245cfb2      h1:CCH4IOTTfewWjGOlSp+zGcjutRKlBEZQ6wTn8ozI/nI=

We can get that at runtime (using https://godoc.org/rsc.io/goversion/version) but for better or worse, that doesn't include that the Git hash of the top-level module, only the deps.

So one thing we could do is add a fake dep to another module (like github.com/tailscale/version-horizon) that we have a bot auto-advance every $INTERVAL, so at least we have a rough date range of what binary people are running when they're running unofficial binaries. Or, if we're already having a bot do this, avoid that indirection and just have the bot auto-commit the latest date to version/version.go every $INTERVAL instead.

Low priority, but we'll probably want better data in the future.

response.title: Figure out tailscale{,d} file paths for non-linux unixes
response.body:
tailscale{,d} is shaping up, and as part of that I'm moving a bunch of paths around:
 - tailscaled state is in /var/lib/tailscale/*
 - tailscaled's unix socket is in /run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock
 - tailscaled's logs buffer (buffering crash dumps for future upload) will is in /var/log/tailscale
 - tailscale CLI's logs config is in ~/.config/tailscale
 - tailscale CLI's logs buffers are in ~/.cache/tailscale

The tailscaled paths are managed by systemd, so they're guaranteed to always exist on daemon startup, and /run/tailscale is guaranteed to be cleaned up on daemon exit.

What's the right place to put these files on *BSD? I'm guessing most of them are already correct, with the possible exception of /run/tailscale -> /var/run/tailscale ?

cc @wardn @martinbaillie as our resident BSD knowers.

response.body: Will review in hour or two.

Going to mildly abort on this, because while I think we want this cleanup at some point, it's actually not on the critical path for rolling out tailscaled - we can store our log buffers in our state dir like animals for a bit, and move them around later.

So, review definitely desired to figure out how we can make this nice, but not urgent.

> Going to mildly abort on this, because while I think we want this cleanup at some point, it's actually not on the critical path for rolling out tailscaled - we can store our log buffers in our state dir like animals for a bit, and move them around later.

I agree it's not urgent, but I also feel dirty for where they're writing now, so it'd be nice to clean up before it's used more widely.
Three positional args of same type isn't ideal at call sites.
What's the alternative? Agreed that it's not ideal, although in practice it's invoked exactly once per binary in main(), so IMO not a massive deal.

It seems like we could get this down to either 0 or 1 arguments: just the collection, if that couldn't even just be automatic based on the binary name. But probably just the collection name is easiest and most explicit.

The stateFile and logsDir seems like they could have automatic locations based on the user. For root, /var/log/*, else $HOME/var/tailscale/logs or something.

The names I picked are not quite accurate, in the sense that `logsDir` actually stores temporary buffers. Their purpose is to buffer data prior to sending to log.tailscale.io, and to record crash goroutine dumps, so that the next process restart can pick it up and send it.

So in that sense it's more temp data than it is logs. We should still try to preserve it somewhat, but it's not extremely precious for long.

On that basis, system user location would be /var/cache/tailscale, state file would be /var/lib/tailscale (alongside tailscaled internal state). For users, ~/.cache/tailscale and ~/.config/tailscale.

Problem: we don't really want to autodetect "system user-ness". At some point I'm going to make tailscaled non-root, at which point the obvious "root is special" rule gets messed up. That's why I wanted some kind of way for the caller to decide where it's storing stuff.

Perhaps that means two constructors? `NewUser`, `NewSystem`? That internally call this `new` with appropriate paths?
Note this logic also has to do the right thing on Windows and Mac. The os.* helpers you pointed out help with that, but we need to think that through also.

`NewUser` and `NewSystem` is also not great for related reasons. That's you as a program author making assumptions about how/where it'll be run.

I'd just pick N OS-specific priority-ordered directories (where N=1 or 2) where you'd like to write state (keys, temp buffers) and then pick the first writable location.

Scanning through dirs is still error-prone in a different way, in that multiple things may end up squashing each others's files :/

How about `New(collection, progName string)`, so that we can inject `progName` into filenames for differentiation?
Stale docs.

response.title: Improve support for running as a non-root user
response.body:
Original title: Re-attempt lock down systemd unit configuration more

The tailscaled systemd service configuration is something I whipped up quickly, based on relaynode's config. It runs as root and unconfined on the system. This is too much privilege.

We should run tailscaled as a `tailscale` system user, with pinhole CAP_* granted to it. Then we can also start screwing down other sandboxing options like ProtectSystem et al.

One prerequisite for this is that we need to use netlink to directly configure the network stack, instead of shelling out to `ip` and `iptables`. That way we can do everything with CAP_NET_ADMIN in-process (although possibly ambient capabilities would let us shell out with appropriate privs as well? I can never remember the capability semantics)

-- 

In the time since this bug, we have added a good number of features that further extend the capabilities that we use, which are often granted by default to root, but not to non-root users.

We can track additional known challenges relating to root dependencies here, with an eye to eventually offering fuller feature support with reduced privileges.

+// Copyright 2019 Tailscale & AUTHORS. All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+package magicsock
+
+import (
+	"fmt"
+	"net"
+)
+
+// derpFakeIPStr is a fake WireGuard endpoint IP address that means
+// to use DERP. When used, the port number of the WireGuard endpoint
+// is the DERP server number to use.
+const derpMagicIPStr = "127.3.3.40"       // 3340 are above the keys DERP on the keyboard
+var derpMagicIP = net.IPv4(127, 3, 3, 40) // net.IP version of above
+
+var (
+	derpHostOfIndex = map[int]string{} // index (fake port number) -> hostname
+	derpIndexOfHost = map[string]int{} // derpHostOfIndex reversed
+)
+
+func init() {
+	// Just one zone for now:
+	addDerper(1, "derp.tailscale.com")
+}
+
+func addDerper(i int, host string) {
+	if other, dup := derpHostOfIndex[i]; dup {
+		panic(fmt.Sprintf("duplicate DERP index %v (host %q and %q)", i, other, host))
+	}
+	if other, dup := derpIndexOfHost[host]; dup {
+		panic(fmt.Sprintf("duplicate DERP host %q (index %v and %v)", host, other, i))
+	}
+	derpHostOfIndex[i] = host
+	derpIndexOfHost[host] = i
+}
+
+// derpHost returns the hostname of a DERP server index (a fake port
+// number used with derpMagicIP). It always returns a non-empty string.
+func derpHost(i int) string {
+	if h, ok := derpHostOfIndex[i]; ok {
+		return h
+	}
+	if 1 <= i && i <= 64<<10 {
+		return fmt.Sprintf("derp%v.tailscale.com", i)
+	}
+	return "derp.tailscale.com"
+}

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

NewUserspaceEngine in wgengine/userspace.go issues a call to CreateTUN, which creates the wg0 interface on first run, but results in an "interface wg0 already exists" on subsequent runs.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Mostly just looking for some context on whether this scenario exists on other platforms and how you'd like it to be handled.  Perhaps a way to handle CreateTUN in which if it already exists, it gets reused.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Looking at the wireguard-go implementation, it looks like they're setting an environment variable after creating the tun, and referencing the file descriptor in the environment variable on subsequent runs. I can issue an "ifconfig wg0 destroy" to clean up the interface on close but that seems a little brute-forcish, and handling it higher up will likely impact all the platforms. I've checked the linux/darwin/windows implementations for an example of how this is handled but it's not immediately apparent from the code.

**Additional context**

logtail...
Starting userspace wireguard engine.
external packet routing via --tun=wg0 enabled
CreateTUN: interface wg0 already exists
Error starting wireguard engine: interface wg0 already exists

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.

+// Package derp implements DERP, the Detour Encrypted Routing Protocol.
+//
+// DERP routes packets to clients using curve25519 keys as addresses.
+//
+// DERP is used by Tailscale nodes to proxy encrypted WireGuard
+// packets through the Tailscale cloud servers when a direct path
+// cannot be found or opened. DERP is a last resort. Both sides
+// between very aggressive NATs, firewalls, no IPv6, etc? Well, DERP.
+package derp
+
+import (
+	"bufio"
+	"encoding/binary"
+	"fmt"
+	"io"
+	"time"
+)
+
+// magic is the derp magic number, sent on the wire as a uint32.
+// It's "DERP" with a non-ASCII high-bit.
+const magic = 0x44c55250
+
+// frameType is the one byte frame type header in frame headers.
+type frameType byte
+
+const (
+	typeServerKey  = frameType(0x01)
+	typeServerInfo = frameType(0x02)
+	typeSendPacket = frameType(0x03)
+	typeRecvPacket = frameType(0x04)
+	typeKeepAlive  = frameType(0x05)
+)
+
+func (b frameType) Write(w io.ByteWriter) error {
+	return w.WriteByte(byte(b))
+}
+
+const keepAlive = 60 * time.Second
+
+var bin = binary.BigEndian
+
+const oneMB = 1 << 20
+
+func readType(r *bufio.Reader, t frameType) error {
+	packetType, err := r.ReadByte()
+	if err != nil {
+		return err
+	}
+	if frameType(packetType) != t {
+		return fmt.Errorf("bad packet type 0x%X, want 0x%X", packetType, t)
+	}
+	return nil
+}
+
+func putUint32(w io.Writer, v uint32) error {
+	var b [4]byte
+	bin.PutUint32(b[:], v)
+	_, err := w.Write(b[:])
+	return err
+}
+
+func readUint32(r io.Reader, maxVal uint32) (uint32, error) {
+	b := make([]byte, 4)
+	if _, err := io.ReadFull(r, b); err != nil {
+		return 0, err
+	}
+	val := bin.Uint32(b)
+	if val > maxVal {
+		return 0, fmt.Errorf("uint32 %d exceeds limit %d", val, maxVal)
+	}
+	return val, nil
+}

+// B32 returns k as the *[32]byte type that's used by the

+
+// B32 returns k as the *[32]byte type that's used by the

+func (k Public) B32() *[32]byte { return (*[32]byte)(&k) }
+
+func (k Private) Public() Public {
+	var pub [32]byte
+	curve25519.ScalarBaseMult(&pub, (*[32]byte)(&k))
+	return Public(pub)
+}
