wgengine/monitor: make Close not block forever on Linux

Signed-off-by: Brad Fitzpatrick <bradfitz@tailscale.com>

response.body: Is this the idiom for a zero time? I've always used `time.Time{}`.
Also confused: I thought that Close() unblocked all readers. Clearly not? Is this a new behavior?

> Is this the idiom for a zero time? I've always used time.Time{}.

It's not a zero time. It's just some time that's in the past, and with the added benefit that it's a time that's safe to convert into a C time_t if needed, if it happens to go that route (and I was too lazy to check).

> Also confused: I thought that Close() unblocked all readers. Clearly not? Is this a new behavior?

The code comments in the package suggested it did (that that was the intention) but it ultimately called through to a sysSocket.Close implementation a few layers down that did have a mutex and deadlocked. There's an open bug (https://github.com/mdlayher/netlink/issues/162) too about this.

response.title: wgengine: add OpenBSD router DNS update handling
response.body:
Idiomatic OpenBSD DNS continues to be classic `resolv.conf` (no fancy `resolvconf` like Linux or some BSDs).

I have tested both the replace and restore funcs and they do work. However `Close()` on the routers does not appear be called in the event of SIGINT/TERMs. I think I can see some interrupt handling logic that would propagate a shutdown through the engine in the old `relaynode` code, but not in `tailscaled`.

Also, I'm getting this out the door in the continued spirit of "merge early, merge often" but I'm happy to add tests and refine error log/rets of the BSD stuff as the codebase matures and settles on technique.

Some notes on the TODO comments being removed:
- Tested and confirmed routes are indeed cleaned up nicely by the OpenBSD network stack upon interface deletion.
- Netlink-style monitoring through `devd` should now be possible to add thanks to https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/pull/41.
- Avoiding prematurely optimising for func reuse across the platforms at this juncture based on a comment in the previous PR.

response.body: @apenwarr, you might also want to weigh in on this, particularly removing the `*wireguard/device.Device` from the Router constructor which nobody was using, except an `if false { ... }` block on Windows. I kept your TODO notes in case it's needed again, but I don't have context for what the problem is/was.

The underlying problem that needs to be solved is the actual packets tailscale uses (in particular, the wireguard UDP packets, but ideally also the control server and logs connections) should *not* be carried over the tunnel. This shows up in particular if you allow routing 0.0.0.0/0, which we currently don't, because of this problem, but it could also be triggered if someone exports the wrong narrower subnet.

In particular, let's say you have a relaynode that exports 192.168.0.0/24 which is your office network. If you bring a tailscale-enabled laptop to the office, now you have two kinds of route conflict:
1) If I want to talk to 192.168.0.5, I have two routes: directly over ethernet, and over tailscale.
2) If I want to talk to the local relaynode, the shortest path is via 192.168.0.x.

Normally we would resolve (1) by giving the tailscale interface higher priority. If there's an encrypted route to somewhere, we should always take it. But for (2) we want the *tailscale* packets to that subnet to be routed directly over ethernet.

To resolve the issue, we can bind the tailscale socket(s) specifically to the ethernet interface, and otherwise have the tailscale interface have a higher precedence.

It's tricky to get this right so I temporarily disabled the code for it on Windows. We're going to have to bring it back because it creates real problems when nodes come in and out of an office.

Linux has a similar problem that needs totally different code (but the same idea) to work around: https://www.wireguard.com/netns/

iOS and macOS have a built-in workaround for this problem: NetworkExtension processes live in a namespace already, and that namespace never routes its packets through itself, which is ideal.

Anyway, I don't have especially strong feelings about whether we do or don't change this API right at the moment. We can always bring it back. But we actually should be thinking pretty strongly about bringing it back very soon since we're talking about connection reliability. Once we implement DERP, if local subnet IP addresses don't work to reach peer nodes and hairpinning is disabled, we'll end up routing to DERP and back just to talk to a machine two feet away on the same wifi network, which is obviously not ideal.
Okay, I've reverted that parameter's removal for now.

response.body:
Hello guys,

I'm trying to deploy Tailscale on Windows, but at this moment I have three machines (machine 1 with linux, machine 2 and 3 with windows), and I can't have connection from/to machine 3.

I'm debuging with ping, machine 2 and 3 have the same ICMP Firewall Rule:
```
Rule Name:                            Allow ICMP

                                      Any     Any
Edge traversal:                       No
Action:                               Allow
Ok.
```

but machine 3 it' not working.

How can I debug it? No ping output, no traceroute, no tcpdump output....


In machine 3 I can only ping 100.101.102.103. 
This is my route table on machine 3:
```
administrator@machine3 C:\Users\administrator> route print -4
...
machine2ip           255.255.255.255   machine3ip   machine3ip      5

machine1ip           255.255.255.255   machine3ip   machine3ip      5
```

There are only one difference between them. Local network is different. Machine 1 and 2 are in the same local network, and machine 3 are in another, but I this that's not the problem...

Any suggestion?

+// Copyright (c) 2020 Tailscale Inc & AUTHORS All rights reserved.
+// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
+// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.
+
+package monitor
+
+import (
+	"fmt"
+
+	"github.com/mdlayher/netlink"
+	"golang.org/x/sys/unix"
+)
+
+const (
+	RTMGRP_IPV4_IFADDR = 0x10
+	RTMGRP_IPV4_ROUTE  = 0x40
+)
+
+// nlConn wraps a *netlink.Conn and returns a monitor.Message
+// instead of a netlink.Message. Currently, messages are discarded,
+// but down the line, when messages trigger different logic depending
+// on the type of event, this provides the capability of handling
+// each architecture-specific message in a generic fashion.
+type nlConn struct {
+	conn *netlink.Conn
+}
+
+func NewConn() (Conn, error) {
+	conn, err := netlink.Dial(unix.NETLINK_ROUTE, &netlink.Config{
+		// IPv4 address and route changes. Routes get us most of the
+		// events of interest, but we need address as well to cover
+		// things like DHCP deciding to give us a new address upon
+		// renewal - routing wouldn't change, but all reachability
+		// would.
+		//
+		// Why magic numbers? These aren't exposed in x/sys/unix
+		// yet. The values come from rtnetlink.h, RTMGRP_IPV4_IFADDR
+		// and RTMGRP_IPV4_ROUTE.
+		Groups: RTMGRP_IPV4_IFADDR | RTMGRP_IPV4_ROUTE,
+	})
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("dialing netlink socket: %v", err)
+	}
+	return &nlConn{conn}, nil
+}
+
+func (c *nlConn) Close() error {
+	return c.conn.Close()
+}
+
+func (c *nlConn) Receive() (Message, error) {
+	// currently ignoring the message
+	_, err := c.conn.Receive()
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, err
+	}

response.title: OpenBSD cannot use non-tunX names for tun interfaces
response.body:
On a Debian stretch box, Tailscale failed to start after installing following [the .deb instructions](https://tailscale.com/kb/1026/install-deb).

Specifically, it failed after running the `systemctl start` step (which silently succeeds), when `relaynode` doesn't appear in the process list per `ps`.

Looking at log output, saw:

```
CreateTUN: invalid argument
Error starting wireguard engine: invalid argument 
```

On this machine, there is already a `wg0` interface from a previous Wireguard non-Tailscale installation.

Upon manually running `relaynode` (i.e., not through systemctl) with `--tun=wg1` (picked arbitrary unused name), Tailscale starts up successfully.

It appears that the systemd service file hard-codes `wg0` in the invocation; I edited the file but am conscious that a future update will clobber it.

response.title: Add builds for other GOOSes to CI
response.body:
CI currently builds GOOS=linux. We should build other platforms, just to make sure we don't let syntax errors and other obvious compile failures rot in the repo.

GOOS=darwin and GOOS=windows don't produce useful binaries, but we can at least check that the packages compile.

We're likely to have GOOS=openbsd and GOOS=freebsd soonish.

OpenBSD tunnel names are prefixed with `tun`.

Controlling the port allows for deterministic configuration of firewall
rules (using `pf` in this case).

Signed-off-by: Martin Baillie <martin@baillie.email>

response.body: MTU is set when the tun device is created in `userspace.go`. We use the default MTU set by wireguard-go, which is 1420. So there should be no need to set MTU here.

Does the OpenBSD network stack delete routes automatically when an interface goes down, or when an interface is destroyed? It probably Just Works right now because worst case either some route adds soft-fail (because the routes already exist), or the routes get cleaned up on shutdown when ts0 is destroyed.

Not sure why it's disabled, but at a glance I suspect the linux implementation might need a bit more work to interop with systems that don't use systemd-resolved. If there is One True Way to do resolv.conf manipulation on openbsd, I think it's fine to do that now. @crawshaw thoughts?

We disabled it because there's no user option to disable it. @apenwarr didn't want installing relaynode to mean you must accept your resolv.conf being overwritten.

From my reading of the systemd docs, as amazing as this is: if you overwrite /etc/resolv.conf, systemd-resolved will respect it. So I believe this is moderately portable.

Ah, I see. What I was referring to was: I think resolved has its own way of providing a "VPN resolver" to it. Failing that, resolvconf is popular for modular assembly. Failing that, replacing /etc/resolv.conf is the best we can do.

response.title: do STUN lookup periodically
response.body:
Copying bug from @apenwarr elsewhere:

> STUN should re-run sometimes, not just at startup time, in case local IP address or NAT changes.
>
> This matters on Linux especially because the local network might not be up at boot time.

We just had a bug report from a user whose ISP gives them a new IP pretty regularly and they had to manual restart the tailscale service for it to unbreak after those ISP changes.

/cc @danderson

response.title: debian: fix changelog generation.
response.body:
It seems changelog generation got broken by moving the code between
corp and OSS repos, because one of the commit SHAs doesn't have an
associated tag.

In the interest of fixing the build, and because we're not yet trying
to upstream the debian package, I fixed this by allowing hash-based
versions to show up in the changelog. This maybe wrong from a
debian standards perspective, but for our current point in life
it'll work until we learn to do it better.

response.title: Support state storage in the backend.
response.body:
In our current codebase, the agent frontend (e.g. CLI, windows UI) owns a user's state and passes it in on startup. There were good reasons for that on Windows, due to limitations of the OS's IPC mechanisms. However, we've decided we need to move the state into the backend.

This change adds support for owned state in LocalBackend, as well as a file-based implementation that `tailscaled` can use. Frontends can choose whether LocalBackend will use purely frontend state, purely backend state, or import frontend state into the backend before use (as a migration path for existing machine keys).

Other existing frontends (Windows, MacOS, iOS UIs) are unchanged for the moment, and continue to pass in state owned by the frontend.

+// identifier for itself, and uses that as the StateKey when talking

response.body: Don't use SetRoutesFunc. It's used only by the mac/ios builds, as a way to bridge Go and Swift together. `router_freebsd.go` should implement Up() and SetRoutes() in terms of FreeBSD APIs or commands (e.g. `ifconfig`, `route`, or equivalent kernel APIs, whatever's idiomatic for the platform).

(to be clear, this is a bug on our end - SetRoutesFunc exists in the cross-platform code as a hack that enables us to build bits of the mac/ios code from Linux, to reduce the amount of breakage - but it's not clearly documented that this is what's happening)

Thanks for the PR! I think we'd want implementations for Up/SetRoutes/Close before merging, otherwise the "freebsd support" is a bit of an empty promise, as tailscaled will come up without configuring its interface or the system routing table.
The implementation for Up() and SetRoutes() is similar to #36, so I'll hold off on this request until that pull lands and verify that they're compatible.

Landed! It'd be cool if all the *bsd end up with compatible code, but don't be afraid to copy/paste for now. Once the per-platform support is fully mature we can start refactoring common stuff, but for right now "anything" is better than "perfect" :)

response.title: Adapt to changing network environments better
response.body:
Overall tracking bug for network change reactivity.

When the network environment changes (e.g. switch from LTE to wifi, NAT gateway reboots and loses all its mappings), nodes should reestablish connectivity gracefully.

We currently adapt in some cases, but not others. We should always notice changes to connectivity, and adapt gracefully to them.

response.title: Improve NAT traversal
response.body:
Meta-bug for getting traffic through more types of NATs.

Our current traversal logic works fairly well with NATs that use endpoint-independent mapping (aka "full cone NAT" to use the old terminology) and endpoint-dependent firewalling. This covers most linux-based routers and basic enterprise NATs.

We don't yet work when both nodes are behind endpoint-dependent mapping (aka "Restricted Cone" or "Port-restricted").

We don't yet work reliably when both nodes are behind the same NAT, but have to hairpin through the NAT device to get connectivity.

response.title: Finish, deploy DERP
response.body:
Tracking bug for deploying DERP, the "Detour Encrypted Routing Protocol".

Tailscale tries to send traffic directly between peers, traversing NATs as needed, but sometimes no path is possible or it takes some time to find a path, so DERP is the ultimate fallback that routes encrypted packets through the cloud.

DERP is somewhat implemented & tested, but not enough, and it's not yet deployed + used.

response.title: Make connectivity always work
response.body:
Tailscale end-to-end connectivity between peers needs to always work, even if the peers have challenging/changing network configurations.

Some high level dependent bugs are:

- [x] [Finish, deploy DERP](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/2), Issue #2 (the fallback cloud proxy for routing encrypted Wireguard packets if all else fails or when a route hasn't yet been created/found through NAT)
- [ ] [Handle more types of NATs](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/3), Issue #3
